item.title: Build a Personal Design System in a Weekend: Palette, Type Scale, Spacing, 5 Components and a README
item.description: You don't need a team to have a design system. Here is a two-day plan to build a small, practical system for your own portfolio, posts and documents, using my GitHub profile system as the case study.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
After reading this, you’ll have a two-day plan to build a small personal design system that makes everything you publish look like it belongs together.

Photo by Firmbee on Pixabay (Pixabay Content License).

Why it matters

Most designers spend their time building systems for clients and almost none on their own work. The result: a portfolio, a LinkedIn banner, a CV and a GitHub profile that each look like a different person made them.

A personal design system fixes that. It doesn’t need to be big. In Building a personal design system from one colour I explained the thinking behind my own palette. This post is the practical version: a weekend plan you can follow.

The idea explained

A personal system has five parts. Each one is small:

  1. Palette: one main colour, one accent, neutrals, and light/dark variants.
  2. Type scale: one or two typefaces and five or six sizes.
  3. Spacing scale: a short list of spacing values (for example 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64).
  4. Five core components: the things you make most often.
  5. README: one page explaining how to use it.

A real example

My own system started from a single violet and a sharp lime accent, with a deep ink colour for text. I use it across my site, GitHub profile, blog covers and documents.

Before, my GitHub profile README was a list of badges in every colour, mixed fonts in images and no clear structure. After applying the system, it uses the same palette, the same heading style and a consistent card layout as the website.

Try it yourself: the weekend plan

Saturday morning: palette (2 hours) - Pick one main colour that feels like you. - Add one accent with strong contrast. - Add an ink (near-black) and two or three neutrals. - Check text contrast with a WCAG checker.

Saturday afternoon: type and spacing (3 hours) - Choose a display typeface and a text typeface (or one family for both). - Build a scale with a ratio such as 1.25: for example 14, 16, 20, 25, 31, 39 px. - Choose spacing steps based on 4 or 8 px.

Sunday morning: five components (3 hours) Pick the five things you make most. Mine are: 1. Button / link style 2. Card (project or post) 3. Section heading with a small label 4. Social post template 5. Cover/banner template

Build each in Figma using only your palette, type and spacing.

Sunday afternoon: README and rollout (2 hours) - Write one page: colours with values, type sizes, spacing, components, do’s and don’ts. - Apply it to one real thing immediately: your GitHub README, LinkedIn banner or CV.

Common mistakes

  • Too many colours. Start with fewer; you can add later.
  • Building components you never use. Five real ones beat twenty theoretical ones.
  • Skipping the README. Without it, you’ll forget your own rules in a month.
  • Not applying it. A system lives only when it’s used.
  • Changing it every week. Give it three months before redesigning.

Summary

  • A personal design system has five parts: palette, type scale, spacing, components, README.
  • Keep each part small and practical.
  • Build the five components you actually use most.
  • Write a one-page README so future you follows the rules.
  • Apply it immediately to one real profile or document.

Sources and image credits

  • Figma variables documentation.
  • WebAIM, contrast checker.
  • All diagrams and mock-ups were made by me for this post.

item.title: Tanvir and the 50/50 Myth: What Work-Life Balance Really Means
item.description: Tanvir works night shifts at a TV channel in Tejgaon and has decided work-life balance is impossible for people like him. Then his grandmother, peeling oranges on a winter afternoon, gives him a better definition. A Friday story.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
A Friday story. The people and places are fictional; the lessons are real.

Tanvir had read the articles. Eight hours of work, eight hours of rest, eight hours of life. He laughed every time.

Tanvir Hasan was 30, a broadcast engineer in the master control room of a TV channel in Tejgaon. His roster rotated: mornings one week, evenings the next, nights after that. Live cricket ran over. Breaking news arrived without asking. Eid meant working while the city celebrated.

“Work-life balance,” he told his cousin Arif over the phone, “is for people with normal jobs.”

Photo by GidonPico on Pixabay (Pixabay Content License).

The guilt

He felt it everywhere. When he missed his nephew’s birthday because of a night shift, he felt guilty about family. When he left the control room on time and a problem appeared an hour later, he felt guilty about work. When he finally had a day off, he spent it asleep, and felt guilty about that too.

Every day was supposed to be balanced. Not one of them was.

Nani’s oranges

One Friday in late November, Tanvir visited his grandmother in Mohammadpur. Nani sat on the veranda in a shawl, peeling oranges, the radio playing old songs.

“You look tired, bhai,” she said.

He told her about the shifts, the guilt, the articles with their perfect eight-eight-eight.

Nani laughed and handed him half an orange. “When your grandfather was building his business, he worked until midnight for two years. When your mother was born, he came home every day for lunch. When I was ill, he closed the shop for a month. Was he balanced?”

“Some years, no,” Tanvir said.

“Over his life? Yes.” She wiped her fingers. “You are measuring the wrong thing. You measure a day. Measure a season.”

A better definition

On the bus home, Tanvir wrote in his phone’s notes:

Control. Some say over when and how I work. He couldn’t choose his shifts, but he could swap with colleagues in advance and plan around the roster.

Recovery. Enough rest that he started each roster week with energy, not exhaustion.

Presence. When he was at work, fully there. When at home, actually home, not half-reading the control room WhatsApp group.

Priorities. Time going to the things he said mattered: his parents, his health, the guitar he hadn’t touched in a year.

Hours weren’t on the list.

The scorecard

That night, he scored himself from 1 to 5 on each.

Control: 3. Recovery: 1. Presence: 2. Priorities: 2.

Recovery was the problem. He’d been treating days off as “catch-up sleep and nothing else”, and he was never really rested.

So he changed one thing. After each night-shift week, he protected the first full day off: sleep until late morning, then a walk by the lake at Dhanmondi, lunch with his parents, and no work messages until the evening.

Three months later

It wasn’t perfect. Some weeks were still brutal. But on the Friday he visited Nani again, he brought his guitar.

“Balanced?” she asked.

“This season,” he said, “more than before.”

Try this week

Score yourself from 1 to 5 on control, recovery, presence and priorities. Pick the lowest score and make one small change, like protecting one evening, one morning or one full day off.

Summary

  • Balance isn’t a daily 50/50 split; measure it over weeks and seasons.
  • Real balance means control, recovery, presence and priorities.
  • Hours matter less than whether you recover.
  • Balance changes with your life stage.
  • Score yourself on the four parts and fix the lowest first.

item.title: Writing the Runbook So Anyone Can Lead at 3 AM
item.description: How to write runbooks and SOPs for broadcast operations that any operator can follow at 3 AM, so the channel stays on air when the expert is not there.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
At 3 a.m., the most experienced engineer in the building is usually asleep at home. Whoever is on shift has to deal with whatever happens, often alone, often tired, sometimes new to the job.

That’s why I think a good runbook is one of the most powerful leadership tools a technical team has. It is your best judgement, written down, available to anyone at any hour. When it’s done well, the night shift doesn’t need you awake. When it’s done badly, they call you, or worse, they guess.

Photo: Building Architecture by Vladimir Kudinov, CC0, via StockSnap.

What a runbook is (and isn’t)

A runbook is a set of step-by-step instructions for specific situations: a feed loss, an encoder failure, a power changeover, a satellite issue, a scheduled maintenance task.

It is not:

  • A manual that explains how the equipment works.
  • A policy document full of “should” and “ensure”.
  • A diary of what happened last time.

It answers one question: “This is happening. What do I do, in what order?”

Write for the tired, new person

The test I use: could someone in their first month, at 3 a.m., under pressure, follow this without calling anyone? That changes how you write:

  • Short numbered steps, one action each.
  • Exact names: the label on the panel, the name on the screen, the button text. Not “switch to the backup source” but “On router panel 2, press BKP-1”.
  • What you should see next: “The tally light on monitor 4 turns red.”
  • What to do if you don’t: “If the picture doesn’t return within 10 seconds, go to step 6.”

Vague steps feel efficient to the writer and impossible to the reader.

Start with the symptom, not the cause

At 3 a.m., nobody knows the cause yet. They know the symptom: black picture, no audio, freeze, colour bars on air, alarm on the encoder. So organise runbooks by what the operator sees:

  • Picture frozen on main output
  • Audio missing on air
  • Satellite uplink alarm
  • Mains power failure

Each one begins with “restore air” steps, then moves to “diagnose and report” steps.

Put the decision points in writing

Good runbooks don’t remove judgement. They tell people where judgement is needed and give them a default:

If you are unsure whether to switch to backup, switch. A backup picture is always better than a frozen one.

Defaults like this are leadership. They decide in advance, on a calm day, what the team should do on a stressful night, and they take the fear out of acting.

Include who to call, and when

Every runbook ends with escalation:

  • Who to call (role first, then name and number).
  • When to call: immediately, after 10 minutes, or at start of business.
  • What to tell them: what happened, what you did, what’s on air now.

This protects both sides. Juniors know they are allowed to call. Seniors receive a clear summary instead of a confused one.

Keep it alive

Runbooks rot. Equipment changes, panels get relabelled, and a step that worked last year becomes wrong. Some habits that keep them useful:

  • Review after every incident. Did the runbook help? Where did people deviate, and why?
  • Have new staff test them. If a newcomer gets stuck, the runbook is wrong, not the newcomer.
  • Date every page and name an owner.
  • Keep them where the work is: printed at the desk and on a shared drive, in case the network is the thing that failed.

Why this is leadership

It’s tempting to see documentation as admin work that gets in the way of “real” engineering. I see it the other way around. A runbook spreads the knowledge of one experienced person to every shift. It lets juniors act confidently. It makes the team less dependent on any single hero.

Leadership isn’t only about being there when things go wrong. It’s about making sure the team is ready when you’re not.

If you want the wider context of how runbooks fit with handovers and checklists, read Running an MCR like a high-reliability operation.

Summary

  • A runbook guides action; it isn’t a manual.
  • Write for a tired, new person.
  • Start with the symptom, not the cause.
  • Put decision points and escalation contacts in writing.
  • Keep it alive after every incident.

item.title: RGB vs CMYK vs Pantone: Why Your Logo Looks Different on Screen and in Print
item.description: The bright red on your screen came back brown from the printer. Here is why RGB, CMYK and Pantone spot colours behave differently, and how to specify a brand colour so it survives every medium.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
After reading this, you’ll know why colours change between screen and print, and how to specify a brand colour so it stays consistent.

Photo by paine_z on Pixabay (Pixabay Content License).

Why it matters

Almost every designer has had the “my red turned brown” moment. The logo looked perfect on screen, the printed banners arrived, and the colour was duller, darker or just different. Clients notice. Brand consistency depends on understanding that screens and printers make colour in completely different ways.

This builds on last week’s post, Colour profiles explained.

The idea explained

  • RGB (additive): screens emit red, green and blue light. Add all three at full strength and you get white. Screens can show very bright, saturated colours because they produce light.
  • CMYK (subtractive): printers lay down cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink in tiny dots. Ink absorbs light; paper reflects what’s left. Many bright screen colours, especially vivid reds, oranges, greens and blues, can’t be reached with four inks. They’re out of gamut.
  • Pantone spot colours: instead of mixing a colour from four inks on paper, the printer uses one ink pre-mixed to an exact formula. Spot colours can reach colours CMYK can’t (including metallics and fluorescents) and stay more consistent between print runs.

So the same “brand red” can be described three ways, and each description is a different physical process.

A real example

Imagine a brand red defined only as #E4002B on screen:

  • On screen (RGB): bright and clean.
  • Printed in CMYK after an automatic conversion: still red, but it can lose brightness and drift slightly towards brown or orange, depending on paper and press.
  • Printed with a matching Pantone spot ink: much closer to the intended colour, because the ink was mixed for it.

The fix isn’t to choose one system. It’s to define the colour in all of them and tell each supplier which one to use.

Try it yourself

Create a simple colour spec for one of your brand colours:

Use Value
Screen (web, apps, social) HEX and RGB
Four-colour print CMYK values (agreed with your printer or from the Pantone guide)
Spot print (signage, packaging, premium print) Pantone number, coated (C) and uncoated (U)
Video Rec.709 RGB (usually the same as screen values)

Then ask a printer for a proof of the CMYK version and compare it with your screen in daylight. You’ll quickly see which colours need adjusting.

Common mistakes

  • Designing print files in RGB and letting the printer’s RIP convert automatically, without a proof.
  • Choosing brand colours only on screen. Check early whether they can be printed.
  • Using one CMYK value for every paper. Coated and uncoated paper give different results.
  • Expecting a perfect match. Screens and paper will never be identical. The goal is consistent and approved, not identical.
  • Forgetting the black. Rich black (CMYK with extra C, M, Y) prints deeper than 100% K alone for large areas, but isn’t suitable for small text.

Summary

  • Screens add light (RGB). Printers subtract light with ink (CMYK).
  • Many bright screen colours can’t be reproduced with CMYK inks.
  • Pantone spot inks are pre-mixed for accuracy and reach colours CMYK can’t.
  • Define every brand colour in HEX/RGB, CMYK and Pantone.
  • Always proof printed colour, on the actual paper.

Sources and image credits

  • Pantone: what is a spot colour.
  • Adobe Help: colour modes in Photoshop and Illustrator.
  • Pantone® and PMS are trademarks of Pantone LLC. Colours shown on screen are approximations of printed colours.
  • All diagrams were drawn by me for this post.

item.title: "Dead Air Is Not an Option": Deciding With 30 Seconds to Act
item.description: What happens in the first 30 seconds of dead air in a TV master control room, and how to make calm, correct decisions under live broadcast pressure.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
Every broadcast engineer knows the phrase: dead air is not an option. A black screen, frozen picture or silent audio is the one failure every viewer notices instantly. When it threatens, you don’t get a meeting. You might get thirty seconds.

Working in Channel i’s Master Control Room has taught me that fast decisions are not about being brave or brilliant. They are about having done most of the thinking before the clock started. This post breaks down how that works.

Photo: Sports stopwatch, timepiece, CC0, via rawpixel.

Decide in advance, act in the moment

The most important decisions in an MCR are made on calm days:

  • What is our backup for each source? Second feed, standby clip, slate, alternative encoder.
  • What is the order of actions? Restore air first, diagnose second.
  • Who is allowed to make which call? An operator shouldn’t need permission to switch to backup.

When those answers already exist, a thirty-second decision becomes a choice between a few prepared options, not an invention under pressure. That is the real job of a leader here: shrink live decisions down to choices that have been thought through.

Restore first, understand later

Engineers love to understand problems. Under pressure, that instinct is dangerous. If the picture is gone, the priority is getting something acceptable back on air: the backup feed, a filler programme, a station slate. Root cause can wait ten minutes. Viewers can’t.

A useful mental line is: “What gets a correct picture to the viewer fastest?” Not “what’s the elegant fix”, not “what caused this”, just that.

Use a simple decision frame

When I have seconds, I run through a short sequence:

  1. What do I see? Confirm the symptom on more than one monitor.
  2. Where is it broken? Source, path or output. This decides which backup helps.
  3. What’s my safest option? The action with the least chance of making it worse.
  4. Act and announce. Do it, say it out loud, and say when you’ll update.

It takes far less time to do than to read. The point is that the steps are the same every time, so the brain doesn’t waste effort deciding how to decide.

Reversible beats perfect

Under time pressure, prefer the decision you can undo. Switching to a backup path is reversible. Rebooting a core device in the middle of a programme often isn’t. Leaders sometimes feel they must find the “right” answer instantly. In reality, a quick reversible step buys time to find the right answer safely.

Trust the person closest to the signal

The person watching the multiviewer often sees the problem first. A team where operators wait for a senior engineer before acting loses precious seconds. Good leadership here means giving clear authority in advance: if the main feed fails, you switch. You don’t need to ask.

Then, after the event, you back that person up, even if their call wasn’t perfect. People only act fast if they know they won’t be punished for acting in good faith.

After the thirty seconds

Once air is safe, the work continues:

  • Log what happened, with times.
  • Keep watching. A fix that holds for one minute isn’t proven.
  • Inform the right people: duty manager, programming, engineering.
  • Hold a short, blameless review once the shift allows.

The review is where the next thirty-second decision gets easier, because the team updates its prepared options.

The lesson for any team

Most leaders don’t face dead air, but many face their own version: a client presentation that breaks, a launch-day bug, an event where the projector fails in front of hundreds of people. The same approach works:

  • Decide your backups before you need them.
  • Restore a good-enough experience first.
  • Prefer reversible steps.
  • Give the people closest to the problem the authority to act.
  • Learn afterwards, without blame.

Good decisions under pressure are rarely made under pressure. They are made earlier, quietly, by people who expected the bad day to come.

Summary

  • Decide in advance so you only act in the moment.
  • Restore air first and understand the cause later.
  • Use a simple frame: confirm, switch, announce, stabilise.
  • Prefer reversible actions over perfect ones.
  • Trust the person closest to the signal.

item.title: Designing Redundancy for 24/7 Transmission: N+1 vs 2N, Failover Testing, and When Each Is Worth the Cost
item.description: N+1 vs 2N redundancy for TV playout and transmission: where each fits, how to test failover properly, and when the extra cost of 2N is worth it.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
Ask any broadcast engineer whether their channel has redundancy and the answer is almost always “yes”. Ask a second question, “when did you last prove the backup takes over by itself?”, and the room goes quieter.

Redundancy isn’t a box you buy. It’s a design decision made separately for every link in the transmission chain, and it only counts when it has been tested. In this post I’ll explain the two most common models, N+1 and 2N, where each one makes sense in a TV facility, and how to test failover without putting the air at risk.

Photo: Satellite dish space technolgy, CC0, via rawpixel.

First, map the chain

Before choosing a redundancy model, draw the path a picture takes from playout to the viewer. In a typical satellite channel in Bangladesh it looks something like this:

  1. Playout server (or automation + server pair)
  2. Master control switcher / branding (logos, tickers, graphics)
  3. Encoder (compression to MPEG-2, H.264 or HEVC)
  4. Multiplexer (if several services share a carrier)
  5. Modulator and upconverter
  6. HPA (high-power amplifier)
  7. Antenna and uplink to the satellite
  8. Plus the things everything depends on: power, reference/sync, network and cooling

Each box is a single point of failure until you decide otherwise. The aim isn’t to duplicate everything. It’s to know, for each box, what happens when it fails and how long the screen stays black.

The vocabulary

  • N is the number of units you need to run the service.
  • N+1 means one spare unit shared across the group. If you need four encoders, you have five, and the spare takes over for whichever one fails.
  • 2N means a complete second copy of everything. Two playout chains, two encoders, two modulators, ideally running in parallel all the time.
  • 1+1 is the 2N idea applied to a single service: one main, one dedicated backup, both live.
  • Hot, warm and cold standby describe how ready the backup is: already running and in sync (hot), powered but needing configuration (warm), or on a shelf (cold).

N+1: efficient, but slower and shared

N+1 is popular for groups of identical equipment, such as encoders for several channels, or HPAs in a multi-carrier uplink.

Strengths

  • Much cheaper than duplicating everything.
  • Works well when units are identical and configuration can be copied automatically.
  • Good for failures that are rare and independent.

Weaknesses

  • Failover is often not instant. The spare has to load the right configuration, lock to the input and start outputting.
  • Only one failure at a time is covered. If two units fail, or the spare is already in use, you’re on air with nothing.
  • The switching logic (a router, a redundancy controller) becomes a new single point of failure.

N+1 is a sensible choice where a short interruption is acceptable and many identical units share the same risk.

2N: expensive, fast, and simpler to reason about

In a 2N design, a main chain and a backup chain run side by side, both producing the signal, and a changeover switch picks one. If main fails, the switch moves to backup in a frame or a few frames.

Strengths

  • Near-instant failover, often invisible to viewers.
  • Independent paths: a fault in one chain doesn’t touch the other.
  • Maintenance becomes safer, because you can work on one chain while the other carries air.

Weaknesses

  • Roughly double the equipment, power and rack space.
  • Divergence: if the two chains aren’t kept identical (same playlist, same graphics, same audio routing), the failover itself causes an on-air error.
  • The changeover switch must be very reliable, and needs its own bypass.

2N is worth it for the parts of the chain where a few seconds of black is unacceptable and where a failure would take down the whole channel: playout, master control and the final transmission path.

A practical rule for deciding

For each link in the chain, ask three questions:

  1. Impact: if this fails, does the whole channel go off air, or only one feature?
  2. Likelihood: how often does this type of equipment fail, and how old is ours?
  3. Recovery time: how long would it take a person to fix it by hand at 3 a.m.?

Then sort the answers:

Situation Usually sensible
Whole channel off air, manual fix takes minutes or more 2N / 1+1 hot standby
Several identical units, short outage acceptable N+1 with automatic switching
Single feature affected (e.g., one graphics layer) Cold spare + documented procedure
Very rare failure, very fast manual fix Spare parts on site, and training

The answer will be different for each channel. A news channel running live most of the day can justify more 2N than a channel that mainly plays out recorded programmes.

Don’t forget the shared dependencies

Two perfect chains can still fail together if they share something. These are the usual suspects:

  • Power. Both chains on the same UPS, the same distribution board, or the same phase. In Bangladesh, where grid interruptions still happen, the generator changeover and UPS autonomy deserve as much attention as any video equipment.
  • Reference / sync. One master sync generator feeding everything. Use a pair with automatic changeover.
  • Network. One core switch carrying control traffic for both chains.
  • Playlists and media. Backup playout that isn’t receiving the latest playlist changes or the new promo that was added ten minutes ago.
  • People and procedures. One person who knows how to force a manual changeover.

Redundancy is only as strong as the most shared component.

Failover testing: the part everyone postpones

An untested backup is a hope, not a system. Testing feels risky because it touches the air, so it gets postponed until a real failure does the test for you.

A safer approach:

  1. Start with the paths that don’t touch air. Test backup encoders, spare units and secondary feeds on monitoring outputs first.
  2. Schedule controlled tests at low-risk times, with the right people present and the editorial team informed.
  3. Write a test procedure: what will be switched, what success looks like, how to roll back, who decides to abort.
  4. Test the automatic path, not just the manual one. Pull the input or power to the main unit and confirm the system switches by itself.
  5. Check what viewers would see: was there a glitch, black, frozen frame, audio drop? How long?
  6. Record the result in the maintenance log, including anything surprising.
  7. Fix divergence you discover. Failover tests often reveal that the backup chain is missing a logo, has different audio levels, or runs an older firmware.

How often? A reasonable starting point is a monthly test for the critical on-air chain and a quarterly test for everything else, adjusted to your own risk and to the manufacturer’s guidance.

Making the case for the cost

Redundancy costs money, and management will ask why. Avoid fear. Use numbers:

  • How much revenue does one minute of commercial airtime earn during peak hours?
  • What are the regulatory and contractual consequences of an outage?
  • What does it cost in reputation when viewers and advertisers see black during a major event?
  • How old is the current equipment, and what’s its likely failure rate?

I’ll write about building that business case in a later post on budgeting for broadcast tech.

The takeaway

  • Map your chain and every shared dependency.
  • Use 2N where an outage takes the channel off air and recovery is slow.
  • Use N+1 where identical units share a risk and a short interruption is acceptable.
  • Keep backups identical to the main chain.
  • Test failover regularly, and treat every test as a chance to learn.

Redundancy doesn’t prevent failures. It decides whether a failure becomes an incident report or a non-event.

Summary

  • Map the chain and every shared dependency.
  • Use 2N where an outage takes the channel off air and recovery is slow.
  • Use N+1 where identical units share a risk.
  • Keep backup chains identical to the main chain.
  • Test failover regularly and learn from each test.

item.title: The Handover: How Shift-Change Communication Prevents Outages
item.description: How a good shift handover in a TV master control room prevents outages: what to pass on, how to write it down and why it is a core broadcast leadership habit.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
Every 24/7 team has a weak point that doesn’t appear on any equipment diagram: the few minutes when one shift leaves and another arrives. Knowledge that lived in one person’s head has to move into another’s, often when the first person is tired and the second hasn’t fully woken up.

In broadcast, that gap is where many problems begin. A feed that was “a bit unstable” at 2 a.m. becomes a frozen picture at 4 a.m. because the next operator never heard about it. I wrote about the operational side of this in Running an MCR like a high-reliability operation. This post is about the leadership side: why handovers fail, and how to build a team where they don’t.

Photo: Hubble Space Telescope Control Room by NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr.

Why handovers fail

Handovers rarely fail because people are careless. They fail because:

  • The outgoing person is tired and wants to leave.
  • “Nothing happened” feels like nothing to say, so small warning signs are skipped.
  • Information lives in many places: a log book, a WhatsApp message, a sticky note, someone’s memory.
  • The incoming person doesn’t ask, because asking can feel like doubting a colleague.

None of these are technical problems. They are communication and culture problems, which makes them leadership problems.

What a good handover contains

A useful handover answers the same questions every time, in the same order:

  1. Current state. What is on air right now, on which path, main or backup?
  2. Open issues. Anything unstable, unusual or “probably fine”.
  3. Changes made. What was switched, restarted, reconfigured or tested this shift?
  4. What’s coming. Live events, schedule changes, maintenance windows, special programmes.
  5. Who to call. Which engineer or vendor is involved in an open issue.

Writing these five headings on a shared sheet or form turns a handover from a casual chat into a structured transfer. The structure protects tired people from their own memory.

Talk and write

A written log alone isn’t enough, and a conversation alone isn’t enough either.

  • Writing creates a record that survives the shift and can be checked later.
  • Talking lets the incoming person ask questions and hear the tone: “it’s fine” said with a frown means something different from “it’s fine” said with a smile.

The best handovers I’ve seen are short, face to face, and walk through the written log together.

The incoming person owns the questions

A rule I like: the handover isn’t finished until the incoming person says it is. That small shift in ownership changes behaviour. The person arriving is responsible for understanding, so they ask. The person leaving is responsible for answering, so they don’t rush off.

As a leader, you make this safe by asking questions yourself, publicly, even when you think you know the answer. When senior people ask “just to confirm”, juniors learn that questions are normal, not an insult.

Repeat back the critical items

Borrowed from aviation and healthcare: for anything that could affect air, the incoming operator repeats it back. “So the backup encoder is on the spare input, and the live programme at 8 needs the second return feed.” It takes ten seconds and catches misunderstandings while they are still harmless.

Handovers between teams, not just shifts

The same idea applies wherever work changes hands:

  • From the scheduling team to master control before a special broadcast.
  • From engineers to operators after maintenance.
  • From a designer to a developer when a brand system goes into an app.
  • From one event volunteer team to the next on a long programme day.

Wherever ownership moves, information can fall through the gap. A short, structured handover with a chance to ask questions closes it.

How to introduce better handovers in your team

If your team’s handovers are informal today, don’t try to fix everything in one meeting:

  1. Agree on the five headings above, or your own version.
  2. Put them in one place, such as a shared sheet, a form or a printed log.
  3. Model it yourself on every shift you work.
  4. Praise good handovers out loud, especially when a small note prevented a bigger problem.
  5. Review after incidents: was the problem mentioned at handover? If not, why not?

Good handovers are invisible on a normal day. On a bad day, they are the reason the next shift already knows where to look.

Summary

  • Handovers fail when they are rushed or unstructured.
  • Cover status, open issues, watch list, events and changes.
  • Talk and write: both matter.
  • The incoming person owns the questions.
  • Repeat back critical items, including between teams.

item.title: Logos With a Second Meaning: FedEx, Amazon, Baskin-Robbins, Toblerone and Why Hidden Symbols Work
item.description: An arrow between two letters. A smile that points from A to Z. A number hidden in initials. Why the best hidden symbols in logos work, and how to use negative space in your own designs without making a puzzle.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
After reading this, you’ll understand why hidden symbols in logos work, and how to use negative space in your own marks without turning them into riddles.

This is part of my Logo Autopsy series. Logos belong to their owners; I describe them here for commentary and link to official sources rather than reproducing them. The diagrams are my own abstract examples.

Photo by tookapic on Pixabay (Pixabay Content License).

Why it matters

Most people see a logo for less than a second. A hidden symbol rewards a second look, and the moment someone notices it (“I never saw the arrow!”) they remember the brand and often tell someone else. Done well, the hidden element also reinforces the brand’s message. Done badly, it’s a clever trick nobody needs.

The idea explained

Hidden symbols usually rely on figure/ground: our brain separates shapes (figure) from the space around them (ground). When the ground itself forms a meaningful shape, the logo carries two messages at once.

Four well-known examples show the main techniques:

  • FedEx (negative space). The wordmark, designed by Lindon Leader at Landor in 1994, hides a right-pointing arrow between the “E” and the “x”, suggesting speed and direction. The arrow is never outlined; it’s simply there once you notice it.
  • Amazon (a symbol with two jobs). The orange curve under the wordmark, introduced in 2000, reads as a smile and also points from the “a” to the “z”, hinting that the store sells everything from A to Z.
  • Baskin-Robbins (a hidden number). In the 2000s identity, the pink parts of the “BR” monogram form the number 31, a reference to the brand’s long-running “31 flavours” idea.
  • Toblerone (a hidden animal). The mountain in the logo contains a bear in its negative space, a nod to the Swiss city of Bern, whose symbol is a bear. In 2023 the packaging was redesigned and the Matterhorn image replaced after part of production moved outside Switzerland, which shows that even hidden meanings depend on the brand’s context.

(As with any widely shared design story, check the official brand pages linked below before quoting dates.)

A real example

What makes these work, and what makes many imitations fail? Compare a hidden symbol that supports the message with one that’s only clever:

The successful ones share four qualities:

  1. The logo works without the secret. FedEx is a clean, readable wordmark even if you never see the arrow.
  2. The hidden element supports the brand promise: speed, choice, variety, origin.
  3. It’s simple. One idea, not three.
  4. It survives small sizes, or at least doesn’t hurt legibility when the detail disappears.

Try it yourself

  1. Write down the one idea your brand should communicate (fast, local, growing, safe).
  2. Find a simple symbol for that idea (arrow, leaf, house, shield).
  3. Set your brand name or initials in a few typefaces, and look at the spaces between and inside letters. Could any of them become that symbol with small adjustments?
  4. Test with five people. Show the logo for two seconds. Ask what they saw. Then ask if they notice anything else.
  5. If nobody can read the name, simplify. Legibility wins.

Common mistakes

  • Forcing it. Bending letters until they’re hard to read just to hide a symbol.
  • Hiding something unrelated to the brand. Clever, but meaningless.
  • Too many secrets. One hidden idea is memorable; three are noise.
  • Ignoring small sizes. Check the logo at favicon size.
  • Accidental hidden shapes. Always look at the negative space for shapes you didn’t intend.

Summary

  • Hidden symbols use figure/ground: the space between shapes becomes a shape.
  • The best ones support the brand’s core message.
  • The logo must still work if nobody notices the secret.
  • Keep it to one simple idea, and test at small sizes.
  • Check your own designs for accidental shapes in the negative space.

Sources and image credits

  • FedEx brand and newsroom; Lindon Leader’s design story has been widely published, including in interviews with design publications.
  • Amazon brand guidelines and trademarks.
  • Baskin-Robbins and Toblerone official sites.
  • All logos are trademarks of their owners. They are described here for commentary only and are not reproduced. Diagrams are my own abstract examples.

item.title: The Week Nusrat Said Yes to Everything
item.description: Nusrat is the designer who never says no: to her boss, to the sales team, to her cousin's wedding card. Then one Thursday night in Banani, everything she promised comes due at once. A Friday story about the overcommitment trap.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
A Friday story. The people and places are fictional; the lessons are real.

Nusrat had a reputation at the agency: if you needed something, ask her. She would always say yes.

It was a good reputation to have, at first. At 27, two years into her job as a graphic designer at a mid-sized ad agency in Banani, Nusrat Jahan was the person everyone liked. The sales team liked her because she never refused a “small favour”. Rafiq bhai, the creative director, liked her because she never complained. Even the office peon, Jalil, liked her, because she once designed his daughter’s school science-fair poster on a Friday.

Photo by 16391475 on Pixabay (Pixabay Content License).

Sunday: five small yeses

On Sunday morning, before her first cup of tea had cooled, the requests began.

“Nusrat, just one Facebook post for the bank client? Ten minutes,” said Kamal from sales.

“Apu, can you check my layout before Rafiq bhai sees it?” asked Shuvo, the new junior.

“Nusrat, we need someone for the pitch deck on Wednesday. You’re good with decks,” said Rafiq bhai, already walking away.

Her phone buzzed: her cousin Ritu, getting married in December, needed a wedding card design “whenever you’re free, no hurry.”

And her main project, the packaging redesign for a tea brand, was due Thursday.

Yes. Yes. Of course. No problem. Sure, apu.

Wednesday: the bill arrives

By Wednesday, the ten-minute Facebook post had taken three rounds of changes. Shuvo’s “quick check” became a two-hour redesign. The pitch deck ate her whole Tuesday. Ritu had sent four reference images and a voice note.

The tea packaging, the project she would actually be judged on, sat untouched.

On Wednesday night, Nusrat left the office at 10:40 p.m. The Metro Rail was nearly empty. She opened her laptop on her knees and kept working until Mirpur 10.

Thursday: the deadline

At 4 p.m. on Thursday, the tea brand’s marketing manager called Rafiq bhai. “Where are the packaging options?”

Rafiq bhai walked to Nusrat’s desk. She had two half-finished options and red eyes.

“Why didn’t you tell me you were overloaded?” he asked, quietly.

“You asked me to do the deck,” she said.

“I asked. You could have told me what it would cost.”

Friday: tea at Karim chacha’s stall

On Friday afternoon, Nusrat met her university friend Mitu at Karim chacha’s tea stall near Mirpur 10. Mitu freelanced, and had learned the hard way how to protect her time.

“You don’t say no,” Mitu said, stirring her tea. “So nobody knows what’s really on your plate. Not even you.”

She took a napkin and wrote three questions:

  1. Does this help my main work, or my team’s?
  2. Do I really have the time, without stealing it from something more important?
  3. Am I the right person, or just the nearest person?

“If any answer is no,” Mitu said, “you don’t have to refuse. You negotiate.”

What Nusrat learned

The next Sunday, Kamal from sales came by with another “ten-minute” post.

“I can do it Tuesday,” Nusrat said, “after the tea packaging is approved.”

When Rafiq bhai asked about another deck, she said: “I can do the deck or finish the packaging revisions this week. Which matters more?”

He looked surprised. Then he nodded. “Packaging. I’ll ask Shuvo to start the deck, and you review it.”

Nobody was angry. If anything, people seemed to trust her more. Her yes, it turned out, was worth more now that it wasn’t automatic.

Try this week

List everything you’ve agreed to in the last two weeks. Mark each one: important, nice to do or shouldn’t be mine. Renegotiate one item from the last list, using “yes, if…”, “not now”, “here’s who can” or “which one first?”

Summary

  • Saying yes to everything feels helpful but quietly damages your priorities and trust.
  • Small requests add up to lost evenings and rushed work.
  • Ask: does it support my goals, do I have time, am I the right person?
  • Replace a flat “no” with “yes, if”, “not now”, “here’s who can” or “which one first?”
  • A protected yes is worth more than an automatic one.

item.title: What a 24/7 Control Room Teaches About Calm Leadership
item.description: What running live transmission in a 24/7 master control room at Channel i teaches about staying calm and leading a team when the stakes are on air.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
There is a particular silence in a Master Control Room when something goes wrong. The monitors are still bright, the clocks still tick, but every person in the room is suddenly listening for one voice: the one that says what happens next.

I work in transmission at Channel i, where the MCR runs every hour of every day. Over hundreds of live broadcasts I have learned that technical skill keeps a channel on air, but calm is what keeps a team working well enough to use that skill. This post is about what calm leadership actually looks like in a room where the clock never stops.

Photo: Operators Desk K-25 & K-27 by usdoe, CC0, via rawpixel.

Calm is not a personality. It is preparation.

People sometimes describe a good MCR operator as “naturally calm”. I don’t think that’s true. Calm is mostly the visible result of three invisible things:

  1. You have seen this failure before, in a drill, a checklist or a previous shift.
  2. You know your first move without thinking about it.
  3. You trust the people beside you to do their part.

When those three exist, a fault becomes a sequence of steps. When they don’t, the same fault becomes panic. So the leader’s job begins long before the incident: rehearsing failovers, writing clear runbooks, and making sure every person knows what “normal” looks and sounds like.

The first ten seconds set the tone

In a live incident, the room copies the first person who speaks. If that voice is loud and rushed, everyone rushes. If it is clear and steady, people steady themselves.

The habit I try to keep is simple:

  • Say what you see, not what you fear. “Main feed is frozen on monitor three” is useful. “Everything’s gone!” is not.
  • Say the first action and who owns it. “I’m switching to backup. You check the encoder.”
  • Say when you will update. “Give me thirty seconds, then I’ll tell you where we are.”

That last one matters more than it sounds. People panic when they don’t know what’s happening. A promised update gives them permission to focus on their own task.

Lower your voice when the stakes go up

This sounds like advice from a parenting book, but it works in broadcast. When pressure rises, I deliberately speak more slowly and a little more quietly. It forces me to think before I talk, and it signals to everyone else that we are still in control.

Calm leaders are not the ones who feel no stress. They are the ones who don’t hand their stress to the team.

Separate the fix from the blame

During an incident, there is only one question: how do we get the right picture back on air? Who caused it, why it happened and what we change are all important, but they belong to later, in a blameless post-mortem.

If someone feels they are being judged in the middle of a fault, they hide information. In a control room, hidden information is the most dangerous kind.

Make “normal” boring, on purpose

The calmest shifts are not the ones with no problems. They are the ones where routine is so well practised that a problem stands out immediately. That means:

  • The same start-of-shift checks, every time.
  • The same way of logging events and changes.
  • The same handover routine between shifts.

Boring routine frees attention. When nothing surprises you in the normal flow, you have energy left for the real surprise.

Look after the people, not just the signal

A 24/7 operation runs on tired humans. Night shifts, festival schedules, election nights and long cricket coverage all wear people down. Leading calmly includes noticing when a colleague is exhausted, covering a break, or simply saying “good catch” after someone spots a problem early.

Teams that feel looked after report problems sooner. Teams that feel watched report them later.

What this means outside a control room

You don’t need an ON AIR light to use these lessons. Any team with real deadlines (a newsroom, a design studio, a product launch, an event) faces moments where everyone looks at one person. The same rules apply:

  • Prepare so that calm is possible.
  • Speak first, clearly and slowly.
  • Fix now, learn later.
  • Make routine boring so surprises are obvious.
  • Look after the people who keep things running.

A control room taught me that leadership is mostly invisible when it works. Nobody watching the channel at home will ever know a fault happened. That is exactly the point.

Summary

  • Calm is prepared, practised and expected, not a trait.
  • The first ten seconds of a fault set everyone’s tone.
  • Lower your voice as the stakes go up.
  • Fix first; review later without blame.
  • Make normal routines boring and look after the people.

item.title: Colour Profiles Explained: sRGB, Display P3, Adobe RGB, Rec.709 and CMYK in One Cheat Sheet
item.description: Which colour profile should you export for the web, social media, print and video? A plain-language guide to sRGB, Display P3, Adobe RGB, Rec.709 and CMYK (FOGRA/SWOP), with a decision flowchart.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
After reading this, you’ll know which colour profile to export for web, social, print and video, and why the wrong one makes colours look dull or strange.

Photo by Pexels on Pixabay (Pixabay Content License).

Why it matters

A colour value like #6B4AFF isn’t a colour on its own. It’s an instruction: “this much red, green and blue”. A colour profile tells the device what those numbers mean. Export the right numbers with the wrong profile and the same file looks vivid on your screen, washed out on a client’s phone and muddy in print.

I deal with this from two sides: as a designer exporting brand files, and as a broadcast engineer, where video has its own colour rules. The good news is that you only need to understand five profiles to make the right choice almost every time.

The idea explained

Every profile describes a gamut: the range of colours it can represent. On a chromaticity chart (the horseshoe of all colours people can see), each RGB gamut is a triangle. A bigger triangle can show more saturated colours.

Here are the five you’ll meet most:

  • sRGB: the standard for the web and most screens since the 1990s. Smallest of the RGB gamuts here, and the safest default.
  • Display P3: a wider gamut used by most recent iPhones, Macs and many Android flagships. Roughly a quarter more colour area than sRGB, especially in reds and greens.
  • Adobe RGB (1998): wider than sRGB in greens and cyans. Popular with photographers who print, but rarely the right choice for screens.
  • Rec.709 (BT.709): the HD television standard. It uses the same primaries as sRGB, but video also uses a limited “legal” signal range and its own gamma. More on that in a later post on broadcast-safe colour.
  • CMYK (FOGRA, SWOP, GRACoL): not one profile but a family describing specific printing conditions: paper, ink and press. FOGRA profiles are common in Europe and Asia; SWOP and GRACoL in the US. Ask your printer which one they use.

A real example

Take a bright violet button colour from a brand palette and export it three ways:

  1. Exported in sRGB with the profile embedded: looks the same in every modern browser.
  2. Exported in Display P3 but the profile stripped (some upload tools do this): the numbers are read as sRGB, and the colour shifts.
  3. Converted to CMYK for print: the most saturated violets fall outside the CMYK gamut, so they become slightly duller. That’s physics, not a mistake, and it’s why print proofs matter.

Try it yourself

Use this decision path for your next export:

Where will it be seen? Export as
Website, email, most social media sRGB, profile embedded
App or site targeting modern Apple devices, with a fallback Display P3 + sRGB fallback
Video for TV or YouTube Rec.709 (check your editor’s project settings)
Commercial print CMYK profile from your printer (e.g., a FOGRA profile)
Photo printing at a lab Ask the lab: often sRGB or Adobe RGB

Then open one of your recent exports in Photoshop (Edit → Assign Profile shows what’s embedded) or check it with an online EXIF viewer. Is the profile what you expected?

Common mistakes

  • Designing in a wide gamut and exporting without conversion. Convert to sRGB on export rather than just labelling.
  • Stripping profiles to save a few kilobytes. Many optimisers remove them; check the settings.
  • Converting to CMYK yourself with a generic profile. Use your printer’s profile, or send RGB and let them convert, if they prefer.
  • Assuming Rec.709 and sRGB are interchangeable. The colours match, but video levels and gamma are different.
  • Trusting one uncalibrated screen. Check on a few devices before approving.

Summary

  • A colour profile tells devices what the colour numbers mean.
  • Use sRGB for web and social unless you have a clear reason not to.
  • Use Display P3 only with a fallback and when you’re sure it will be shown properly.
  • Use Rec.709 for video projects; it shares sRGB’s colours but not its levels.
  • For print, use the CMYK profile your printer gives you.
  • Always embed the profile and check the export on more than one screen.

Sources and image credits

  • International Color Consortium (ICC), about ICC profiles.
  • ITU-R, Recommendation BT.709.
  • Apple Developer documentation on wide colour (Display P3).
  • All diagrams were drawn by me for this post. Gamut shapes are simplified for explanation, not measured data.

item.title: Case Study: Building khanfarhana.info, a Brand, a Community and an Academy in One WordPress Theme
item.description: How I designed and hand-coded one WordPress theme that holds a personal brand, a fellowship, an opportunities board, a press room and a full learning platform with payments, and that her team runs without a developer.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
Some websites are a single thing: a shop, a portfolio, a blog. khanfarhana.info had to be five things at once and still feel like one.

Khan Farhana is a youth leader and digital inclusion champion. Her work reaches people through LinkedIn, television, newsletters, a leadership fellowship, public opportunities and, more recently, online courses. Before this project, all of that lived in different places. The website’s job was to bring it under one roof, in one design, and to let her team keep it current without calling a developer for every change.

I handled the whole project: design, front-end, WordPress engineering, the admin experience and SEO. This post walks through how it came together, the decisions that shaped it, and the problems I had to solve on the way. You can also see the visual case study on the site itself.

Photo: Web Design Desk, CC0, via rawpixel.

The brief

The site needed to do a lot:

  • A personal-brand homepage with real storytelling, not just a photo and a bio.
  • Programme pages that turn interest into applications, starting with the Leadership Fellowship.
  • A press room and stories for TV interviews, radio, print features and long-form programme stories.
  • An opportunities board that anyone can contribute to.
  • A learning platform with payments, where students enrol in free or paid courses and earn certificates.

And one rule sat over all of it: the team must be able to edit everything themselves. Headings, cards, buttons, images, dates, cohort names. If an edit needs a developer, the site slowly goes out of date.

The big decision: one hand-coded theme, no page builder

The usual way to build a site like this in WordPress is to stack a page builder, a theme framework and a dozen plugins: one for courses, one for forms, one for directories, one for SEO. It works on day one. It gets slower and more fragile every time something updates.

I went the other way and built a single hand-written theme: plain PHP, CSS and JavaScript, with WooCommerce for payments and almost nothing else. That choice drove everything that followed:

  • Speed. No builder means no builder CSS, no nested wrapper divs and no scripts loaded “just in case”.
  • Consistency. Every page uses the same components, so the design can’t drift as the team adds content.
  • Control. Nothing breaks because a third-party builder pushed an update.

The trade-off is obvious: everything a builder gives you for free, like editable sections, I had to build myself. That’s where most of the work went, and it’s the part I’m proudest of.

Four goals that shaped every page

  1. One home for everything. Brand, programmes, press, newsletters, opportunities and courses under one design.
  2. Run by the team, not a developer. Guided admin fields instead of code.
  3. Fast on a phone. Most visitors arrive from social media on mobile, so layouts, images and fonts are built mobile-first.
  4. Easy to find and trust. Clean structured data, breadcrumbs and a summary that AI assistants can read, so search engines and assistants describe the site correctly.

A light, editorial design language

The design is deliberately calm. Airy white layouts, a serif headline with one italic accent word, and a thin rainbow strip borrowed from the UN Sustainable Development Goals that quietly signs every section. It ties the site to the causes Khan Farhana works on without shouting about it.

The palette stays restrained so photos, press cards and programme content do the talking:

Colour Hex Role
Navy #19486A Primary, headings and buttons
Sky #26BDE2 Links and highlights
Crimson #C5192D Accents and calls to action
Ink #1A1A2E Body text

Typography is a three-font system, each with a clear job:

  • Fraunces for headlines, with its italic used for the single accent word.
  • Plus Jakarta Sans for the interface and body text.
  • BCC Purno for Bangla, loaded only when Bangla text is actually on the page (more on that below).

The build, page by page

1. A homepage that tells a story

The homepage runs like a short biography: a hero, a “Who am I” section, a scrollable timeline covering a decade of impact, the career journey, impact counters, services and a pinned profile card.

Every one of those blocks has its own admin editor. If a new milestone happens, the team adds it to the timeline. If a number grows, they update the counter. The story can change without touching code.

2. A programme page that drives applications

The Leadership Fellowship page has stats, career tracks, a cohort timeline and an apply flow. It’s fully editable, including the cohort name, dates and call-to-action buttons, so a new intake is an admin task, not a redesign.

3. The Opportunities Hub

This is a searchable directory of jobs, scholarships, fellowships and internships, built as its own content type with categories and deadlines. Three details make it work in practice:

  • Visitors can post opportunities through a public form.
  • The team moderates submissions from an approval queue in the admin.
  • Listings close automatically when their deadline passes, so the board never fills up with dead links.

4. Press and media coverage

TV interviews, radio, print and online features appear as clean cards with the outlet, date and an external link. They’re managed as their own content type, so adding a new feature is a form, not a page edit.

5. Featured stories

Long-form stories of programmes and events, each with its own template, structured data and share tools.

6. A blog with reader submissions

A fast reading experience with categories, search and comments, plus a front-end form that lets guest authors submit posts for review. The community can contribute without needing a WordPress account with editor rights.

7. KF Academy: a learning platform of its own

This was the largest piece. KF Academy lets students and instructors sign in separately, enrol in free or paid courses, learn through lessons, quizzes and assignments, and earn verifiable certificates. Sign-up uses an email one-time password.

It’s built natively in the theme, with no third-party LMS plugin. Under the hood that means instructor and student roles, progress tracking and nine purpose-built database tables, with WooCommerce handling payments.

Built for the phone first

Every page reflows cleanly down to small phones: larger touch targets, stacked layouts, no sideways scrolling, and menus that open in one tap.

Under the hood

An admin built for non-developers

The theme ships with more than 45 admin screens, one for each page and section. Instead of asking editors to remember URLs, every button link has a destination picker: choose a page from a list, or paste a custom link. It sounds small. It removes the most common way editors break a site.

A live ticker for OBS

Khan Farhana also streams. The theme includes a transparent overlay page at /ticker/ that can be added to OBS as a browser source. It re-reads its settings about every 15 seconds, so an edit in the admin reaches a running broadcast without restarting anything. Coming from broadcast engineering, this was a fun crossover to build.

SEO and AI-ready

  • Schema.org JSON-LD for Person, Organization, WebSite, breadcrumbs and articles.
  • Visible breadcrumbs that always match the markup, so what users see and what search engines read never disagree.
  • A /llms.txt summary, so AI assistants have a clean, accurate description of who she is and what the site offers.

Performance by design

  • Image dimensions and lazy loading are added at render time across the theme.
  • CSS and JavaScript are minified.
  • The Bangla font loads only when Bangla text is on the page.

Safe to operate

One-click maintenance mode, a branded login screen, one-time data migrations, and demo content that can be imported and removed in one click.

Motion with restraint

Gentle scroll reveals and counters appear only where they help, and they switch off for visitors who prefer reduced motion or have Data Saver turned on.

Problems I ran into, and how I solved them

Every real project has a list like this. These five taught me the most.

1. Garbled apostrophes and ampersands on the homepage. Text in the homepage timeline was being escaped twice on save, so an apostrophe would turn into visible code. I fixed it at the source, then wrote a one-time, repeat-safe migration that cleaned the existing content. Nobody had to retype anything.

2. Images popping in and the page jumping. Many hand-coded images had no width and height, so browsers couldn’t reserve space for them and the layout shifted as they loaded. A small render-time layer now adds dimensions and lazy loading across the whole theme, instead of fixing images one template at a time.

3. Bangla text without a heavy font. Loading a full Bangla font on every page would slow down the English pages for no reason. BCC Purno is mapped to Bangla characters only, using a unicode-range rule and size-adjust. English keeps its own typeface, the two scripts sit at a matching visual size, and the Bangla font is fetched only when it’s needed.

4. Wide layouts breaking on small phones. A few grids pushed the page wider than the screen. Grids now use minmax(0, 1fr), long words wrap safely, and horizontal overflow is clipped. Then I checked every template at phone, tablet and desktop widths.

5. Replacing a plugin without losing payments. The course platform started on a third-party LMS plugin and moved to the native one. The risk was breaking checkout for paid courses. The solution: each paid course gets a hidden, synced WooCommerce product, so carts, orders and receipts kept working exactly as before.

The outcome

  • One theme, no page builder. Everything on the site is plain, hand-written PHP, CSS and JavaScript. There is nothing to break when a builder updates.
  • A team that can run it alone. A 32-page Admin Panel Operation Guide ships with the theme, so new editors can learn every screen.
  • Room to grow. New pages, courses, programmes and opportunities are added from the admin. The structure doesn’t change.

What I’d tell anyone building a site like this

  1. Design the admin as carefully as the front end. The people who edit the site every week are users too. Guided fields and a destination picker did more for the site’s long-term health than any visual flourish.
  2. Fix problems at the source, then migrate. Patching symptoms template by template leaves landmines. Fixing the cause and running a one-time, repeat-safe migration cleans up the past and protects the future.
  3. Own the critical paths. Payments and courses are the parts that hurt most when they break. Building the LMS natively, with WooCommerce only where it’s strongest, made those paths predictable.
  4. Write the manual. A site the client can’t operate is a site that stops changing. The operation guide is part of the deliverable, not an extra.

Visit the live site at khanfarhana.info, and see the screens in the visual case study. If you need a site that your own team can run, get in touch.

Summary

  • Start from a clear brief: brand, community and academy.
  • One hand-coded theme can replace a heavy page builder.
  • Four goals shaped every page decision.
  • A light, editorial design language keeps it readable.
  • Solve real problems as they come and document them.

item.title: Running an MCR Like a High-Reliability Operation: Shift Handovers, SOPs and Checklists That Prevent On-Air Errors
item.description: Run a broadcast master control room like a high-reliability operation: shift handovers, SOPs, checklists and a no-blame culture that prevent on-air errors.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
Most on-air errors don’t start with broken equipment. They start with a small gap between people: a shift that didn’t hear about a flaky feed, a step skipped because “we always do it this way”, a live event that changed at the last minute and nobody wrote it down.

In my work at Channel i, I’ve learned that the equipment in a Master Control Room (MCR) is usually the easy part. The hard part is making a 24/7 room behave the same way at 3 p.m. on a calm Tuesday and at 3 a.m. during a breaking-news overrun, with different people on every shift.

Other industries solved this problem long ago. Hospitals, airlines, air traffic control and power plants operate in conditions where small mistakes become serious very quickly, yet they make remarkably few of them. Researchers call them high-reliability organisations. This post is about borrowing their habits for broadcast: shift handovers, standard operating procedures (SOPs) and checklists.

Photo: Close checklist wooden surface, CC0, via rawpixel.

What “high reliability” actually means

The idea comes from organisational research, most famously Karl Weick and Kathleen Sutcliffe’s work on how these organisations stay safe. They describe five habits of mind. Each one maps neatly onto an MCR:

  1. Preoccupation with failure. Treat every small glitch as a warning, not as luck. A single dropped frame on a backup feed is information.
  2. Reluctance to simplify. “It’s probably the encoder again” is how real causes get missed. Look at what actually happened.
  3. Sensitivity to operations. Know what’s happening on the floor right now, not just what the schedule says should be happening.
  4. Commitment to resilience. Expect things to go wrong and practise recovering from them quickly.
  5. Deference to expertise. In a fault, the person who knows the system best leads, whatever their job title.

None of this needs new equipment. It needs routines that make these habits automatic, which is exactly what handovers, SOPs and checklists are for.

Shift handovers: where most knowledge gets lost

A 24-hour room changes hands several times a day. Every handover is a moment where information can disappear. The outgoing operator knows that the remote feed from the stadium kept breaking up, that the 8 p.m. programme was replaced, that the backup playout server rebooted itself once. If that knowledge doesn’t cross the handover, the next shift rediscovers it the hard way, usually on air.

Make handovers written and structured

Spoken handovers are better than nothing, but they depend on memory and mood at the end of a long shift. Healthcare uses structured formats such as SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) for exactly this reason. For an MCR, I use a simple written structure:

  • On air now: what’s playing, what’s coming in the next hour, any live events scheduled.
  • Changes: schedule changes, replaced programmes, new ad breaks, late material.
  • Known issues: anything flaky, even if it recovered (feeds, encoders, graphics, power, network).
  • Workarounds in place: anything temporary, like a source routed manually or a backup chain left on air.
  • Pending actions: calls to return, tickets raised, engineers on their way.
  • Watch for: the one or two things the next shift should keep an eye on.

It takes five minutes to write and saves far more. It also creates a record: when someone asks next week why the backup chain was on air on Thursday night, the answer is there.

Overlap, don’t just swap

A good handover has a few minutes of overlap where both operators are in the room and both are watching the output. The incoming operator reads the written handover, asks questions, and only then takes over. The rule I like is simple: you haven’t handed over until the other person says “I have it.”

Never hand over in the middle of a critical event

If a live event or a known risky transition is minutes away, the outgoing shift stays until it’s done. Handing over a live programme halfway through is how cues get missed.

SOPs: decide once, not at 3 a.m.

Faults rarely give you time to think. When the main feed drops during a live programme, the operator needs to act in seconds. That’s not the moment to work out from first principles which way to switch.

A standard operating procedure decides in advance, when everyone is calm, what the right response is. In my team, writing technical SOPs and troubleshooting guides for our common faults cut problem-resolution time by about 35%. Most of the time saved wasn’t technical. It was the minutes people used to lose deciding what to do and who to call.

What a good MCR SOP looks like

The SOPs that actually get used share a few features:

  • One page, one situation. “Main playout failure”, “loss of live contribution feed”, “audio missing on air”. Not one giant manual.
  • The first action at the top. Usually “protect the air”: switch to backup, cut to a slate or put up filler. Diagnosis comes after viewers are safe.
  • Short, numbered steps with the exact names of buttons, sources and devices as they appear in the room.
  • Decision points made explicit. “If the backup is also failing, go to step 6.”
  • Who to call, with numbers, and when to escalate.
  • How to return to normal, because switching back is when the second error often happens.
  • A last-reviewed date and an owner, so stale SOPs get noticed.

Keep them where people are

An SOP on a shared drive nobody can find during a fault is useless. The ones that matter most should be printed and within reach of the operator’s chair, and also available digitally. The test is simple: could a new operator find and follow it in under a minute, with an alarm going off?

Update them after every incident

Every real fault is a free test of an SOP. If people had to improvise, the SOP was missing something. Updating it right after the event, while memories are fresh, is how the procedures stay alive.

Checklists: the cheapest reliability tool there is

Atul Gawande’s The Checklist Manifesto popularised a point that aviation learned decades earlier: skilled people still forget simple steps, especially under pressure or routine. Checklists catch those slips.

There are two styles, and both have a place in an MCR:

  • Read-do checklists: you read each step and do it, in order. Good for rare or complicated procedures, like a planned switch to a backup uplink path.
  • Do-confirm checklists: you do the work from memory, then stop and confirm nothing was missed. Good for routine tasks experienced operators do daily.

Checklists I’ve found worth having

Start of shift (do-confirm):

  • Read the handover and ask questions.
  • Confirm off-air monitoring is working and matches the output.
  • Check main and backup chains are both healthy.
  • Check audio loudness meters and alarms are live.
  • Review the next few hours of the playlist, especially live events and transitions.

Before a live event (read-do):

  • Every source tested end to end, including the return feed to the venue.
  • Backup source or filler programme ready and cued.
  • Graphics, lower thirds and tickers checked on the actual output.
  • Communication with the production gallery and the remote team confirmed.
  • Timing agreed: start time, breaks and hard out.
  • Who does what if the main feed fails, said out loud.

Planned changeovers and maintenance (read-do):

  • Is anything live or critical coming up? If yes, wait.
  • Backup confirmed healthy before touching the main.
  • One change at a time, with the result checked on air after each one.
  • A second person watching the output during risky steps.
  • Everything returned to normal and written in the handover.

Keep checklists short

A checklist that takes twenty minutes gets skipped. The best ones fit on one card and only include the steps that are both important and easy to forget. Everything else belongs in training, not on the list.

Two people for risky actions

Aviation uses “challenge and response”: one person reads, the other confirms. In an MCR, the equivalent is simple: for actions that can take the channel off air (switching transmission paths, restarting a playout server, changing routing during a live event), a second person watches the output and confirms each step. It feels slow. It’s much faster than recovering from a mistake that went to air.

Watch the right things, and only the right things

Sensitivity to operations depends on monitoring, but more monitoring isn’t automatically better. A multiviewer wall full of tiny pictures and an alarm panel that beeps constantly teach operators to ignore both. That’s alarm fatigue, and it’s a known problem in hospitals too.

What helps:

  • Make the on-air output and off-air return the biggest pictures in the room.
  • Show audio meters and loudness clearly next to the output.
  • Tune alarms so they mean something: silence, black, freeze and loss of signal on air should be loud and unmistakable; minor warnings shouldn’t sound the same.
  • Review alarm noise regularly and remove the ones nobody acts on.

Learn from near misses, without blame

The most valuable events in a reliable operation are the ones where nothing reached air: the feed that dropped during a promo instead of during the news, the wrong clip caught in preview. These near misses are free lessons.

I find two practices make the biggest difference:

  • A near-miss log in the handover notes: what almost happened and what caught it.
  • Blameless reviews after real incidents: what happened, why it made sense to the people involved at the time, and what we’ll change. The goal is a better system, not a guilty person. If people expect blame, they stop reporting near misses, and the organisation goes blind.

Practise failure on purpose

Redundancy only works if it’s tested. A backup chain nobody has switched to in six months is a hope, not a plan. Regular, planned failover drills (during quiet hours, with everyone aware) keep both the equipment and the people ready. New operators should run their first failover in a drill, not during a live news bulletin.

This connects directly to the preventive maintenance routine I described in Inside a Master Control Room. In our team, steady maintenance cut system downtime by around 30% and helped us reach 99.99% uptime across more than 800 live broadcasts. The hardware matters, but the routine around it matters more.

Look after the people

Every procedure above assumes an alert operator. Night shifts, long live events and back-to-back overruns wear that down. Reliable operations plan for fatigue: sensible shift lengths, proper breaks during long events, and the expectation that anyone can ask for a second pair of eyes without it being a weakness.

A simple starting point

If your MCR doesn’t have these routines yet, you don’t need to build everything at once. Start with three things:

  1. A written handover template, used at every shift change.
  2. One-page SOPs for your three most common faults, printed and within reach.
  3. A pre-live checklist for every live event.

Then review them after every incident and near miss. Within a few months, the room starts to feel calmer, faults get shorter, and the channel stays on air through problems that used to make it go dark.

The audience never sees any of this. That’s the point.

Summary

  • Borrow habits from high-reliability organisations.
  • Make shift handovers structured, spoken and written.
  • Decide procedures once in SOPs, not at 3 a.m.
  • Use checklists and two-person checks for risky actions.
  • Learn from near misses without blame and practise failure.

item.title: Inside a Master Control Room: How a TV Channel Stays on Air 24/7
item.description: How a TV master control room keeps a channel on air 24/7: playout, monitoring, transmission and the daily habits that prevent dead air, from Channel i's MCR.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
Most people only notice a television channel when something goes wrong: a frozen frame, a second of black, audio that suddenly jumps in volume. That is the point. A Master Control Room (MCR) exists so that nobody watching ever has to think about it.

I work in transmission at Channel i, Bangladesh’s first digital satellite television network. My job sits at the last stop before the signal leaves the building. Over the past two years I’ve supported more than 800 live broadcasts, and the most important thing I’ve learned is that staying on air is less about heroics and more about boring, repeatable habits.

This post walks through what an MCR does, how a signal travels from a playlist to a satellite, and the routines that keep a 24/7 channel stable. I’ll describe a typical setup rather than any one station’s exact configuration.

Photo: Little League Softball World Series, CC0, via rawpixel.

What a Master Control Room is for

A newsroom or production gallery makes programmes. The MCR sends them. It is the place where every source a channel might put on air comes together and gets turned into one continuous, legal, correctly timed output.

On a normal day the MCR is responsible for:

  • Playout: running the schedule of programmes, adverts, promos and station idents exactly on time.
  • Live switching: taking live feeds from studios, outside broadcasts and remote reporters at the right moment.
  • Branding and graphics: the channel logo, tickers, “live” bugs and lower thirds that sit on top of the picture.
  • Quality control: watching picture and sound for faults before viewers see them.
  • Compliance: making sure audio loudness, captions and logging meet the rules the channel has to follow.
  • Transmission: handing the finished signal to the encoders and uplink chain that put it on the satellite.

If production is the kitchen, the MCR is the pass where every plate is checked before it leaves.

Following the signal, step by step

It helps to think of the chain as a series of handovers. Every handover is a place where something can fail, so every handover has a way to be watched and, ideally, a backup.

1. Ingest and the playlist

Programmes arrive as files from editors, producers and agencies. They are ingested into a media server, checked for format and length, and placed into a playlist that the traffic and scheduling team has built for the day. A good playlist is not just a list of clips. It holds the exact durations, the secondary events (graphics, logo changes, ad triggers) and the points where live content will interrupt the recorded schedule.

2. Playout automation

Automation software reads the playlist and drives the playout servers and switchers frame by frame. Humans can’t reliably hit a transition at 20:59:59:24 every day; automation can. The operator’s job becomes supervising the automation: preparing live events, adjusting timings when a live programme overruns, and taking over manually when something unexpected happens.

3. The master switcher and branding

The output of playout runs through a master control switcher, where live sources can be cut in and graphics are layered on top. Brands such as Grass Valley, Ross Video, Imagine Communications and Harris are common in this part of the chain.
