This is also where the channel’s on-screen identity lives, which is one reason I care so much about broadcast graphics as a designer. A logo bug that looks good in a brand guideline can still fail on air if it flickers on interlaced pictures or disappears against a bright background.

4. Live contribution

Live content can come from a studio in the same building or from a reporter on the other side of the country. Remote feeds often arrive over bonded cellular systems from vendors such as LiveU and TVU Networks, which combine several mobile connections into one stream, or over dedicated fibre and satellite links. Each contribution path has its own delay, its own failure modes and its own monitoring.

5. Encoding, multiplexing and uplink

The finished baseband signal is compressed by encoders, packed into a transport stream alongside audio and data, and handed to the modulation and uplink chain. From there it goes up to a satellite and back down to cable operators and home receivers across the footprint. Encoders and multiplexers from companies like Harmonic and Ericsson are typical here.

6. Monitoring the return

The MCR doesn’t stop watching once the signal leaves. A good room also monitors what comes back: the signal received off-air through a receiver, so the team sees what viewers see, including any problems introduced after the building.

The quiet standards behind a “normal” broadcast

A surprising amount of MCR work is invisible compliance.

Loudness. Viewers hate adverts that are louder than the programme around them. Broadcasters measure loudness over time rather than just peak levels, using standards such as EBU R128 (a target of −23 LUFS in Europe) or ATSC A/85 (−24 LKFS in the United States). Whatever target a channel uses, the habit is the same: measure, correct at ingest, and watch the meters on air.

Ad insertion triggers. When a programme hits an ad break, cable operators and distribution partners may want to insert their own local adverts. Automation signals those breaks with cue messages. Inside the building they often travel as SCTE-104 messages in the video signal, and encoders turn them into SCTE-35 markers in the transport stream. If those markers are wrong, partners insert adverts in the middle of a news report.

Logging and recording. Most channels must keep a recording of what actually went to air. When there’s a complaint or a dispute, the log is the evidence.

Redundancy: assume everything will fail

The single most useful mindset in an MCR is that every component will fail eventually. The goal is to make each failure small, quick to notice and quick to recover from.

That usually means:

  • Main and backup playout chains, running in parallel, with a changeover switch that can move to the backup in a frame.
  • Dual power to critical equipment, backed by UPS units and generators.
  • Redundant network and signal paths, so a single cable or switch port can’t take the channel off air.
  • Backup content ready to play, such as a filler programme or a slate, for when a live feed drops without warning.

Redundancy only works if it is tested. A backup chain nobody has switched to in six months is a hope, not a plan.

The habits that matter more than the equipment

Equipment gets the attention, but in my experience the difference between a stable channel and a fragile one is the routine around it.

Preventive maintenance. Fans clog, drives wear out, cables get bumped. Scheduled checks of fans, storage, redundant power supplies and connections catch problems while they are still cheap. In our team, a steady preventive maintenance routine cut system downtime by around 30% and helped us reach 99.99% uptime.

Written SOPs. At 3 a.m., during a fault, nobody should be improvising. I’ve written technical standard operating procedures and troubleshooting guides for common faults: what to check first, which way to switch, who to call. Clear SOPs cut our problem-resolution time by about 35%, mostly because people stopped losing minutes deciding what to do.

Clean handovers. A 24-hour room changes hands several times a day. A short written handover (what’s scheduled, what’s flaky, what changed) prevents the classic mistake of one shift not knowing what the previous shift worked around.

Rehearsing live events. Before a big live broadcast we check every source, every return path and every graphic. Most live failures I’ve seen were visible in a rehearsal that someone decided to skip.

Watching what viewers see. Multiviewer walls, off-air receivers and audio meters are only useful if someone is actually looking at them. Good rooms make the important signals large and alarm loudly when something is wrong.

Where MCRs are heading

The traditional MCR is built around SDI cables and dedicated hardware. That is changing. More channels are moving video around the building as IP traffic, using standards such as SMPTE ST 2110, and some playout is moving into software running on standard servers or the cloud. Remote production lets a single control room run events in several locations.

The technology is changing quickly, but the job stays the same: get the right pictures and sound to air, on time, every time, and notice problems before the audience does. I wrote more about the SDI-to-IP shift in From SDI to IP.

What this taught me as a designer

Working in an MCR has changed how I design. Broadcast teaches you that design is only finished when it survives real conditions: a logo on a noisy picture, a lower third read from across a room, a ticker running for twelve hours straight. It also taught me to value clear checklists and calm, repeatable systems, which turns out to be exactly what a good design system is.

If you’re curious about broadcast engineering, the best advice I can give is to spend time in front of a multiviewer and simply watch. Every fault you see once is a fault you’ll catch faster the next time.

Summary

  • The MCR is the last check before a signal reaches viewers.
  • The signal flows through playout, master control, encoding and transmission.
  • Quiet standards like loudness and timing keep broadcasts normal.
  • Redundancy assumes everything will fail.
  • Habits and checklists matter more than equipment.

item.title: AI in My Design Workflow: Where It Helps and Where It Doesn't
item.description: A practical look at using AI tools for briefs, research, ideation, image editing and code, plus the parts of design I still won't hand over.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
AI tools have changed how I work faster than any software change I can remember. Some days they save me hours. Other days they produce confident nonsense that takes longer to fix than doing the job myself.

After a lot of trial and error across brand design, social media work, app interfaces and code, I’ve settled into a clear split: AI is excellent at some parts of the design process and poor at others. Here’s where I use it, where I don’t, and the rules I follow to use it responsibly.

Photo: Office Work by energepic.com, CC0, via StockSnap.

Where AI genuinely helps

1. Turning messy input into a clear brief

Clients rarely send a brief. They send a voice note, three WhatsApp messages and a screenshot of a competitor. A language model is very good at turning that into a structured summary: goals, audience, deliverables, deadlines and open questions.

I never send that summary as-is. I use it as a first draft, correct it, and then confirm it with the client. It saves me twenty minutes of organising and makes sure I don’t miss a requirement buried in a message.

2. Research and first-pass understanding

When I start working with a new industry, AI tools help me get oriented quickly: what terms people use, what competitors typically emphasise, what questions I should ask. It’s a starting point for real research, not a replacement for it. Anything factual gets checked against primary sources before it influences a design.

3. Exploring directions quickly

Image generation tools are useful early in a project for exploring mood and direction: lighting, colour atmosphere, composition ideas for a campaign. I treat these images as sketches. They help a client react (“warmer”, “less busy”, “more local”) before I spend time building the real thing.

What I don’t do is present generated images as finished brand assets. More on that below.

4. Image editing chores

AI-assisted features in tools like Photoshop’s generative fill are genuinely useful for production chores: extending a background to fit a wider banner, removing a distracting object, cleaning up a product shot. These are tasks that used to take careful manual work and now take minutes, though I still check every edge closely.

5. Copy variations and translation drafts

For social media campaigns I often need many variations of a headline or caption. AI can produce options quickly, which I then edit for tone and accuracy. For Bangla, I’m especially careful: AI translations can be grammatically fine but sound unnatural, so a native reader (usually me) rewrites them. I covered the typography side of bilingual work in Designing Bilingual Brands.

6. Code and automation

This is where AI has changed my work the most. I use AI assistants to write and debug the scripts that generate my GitHub profile cards, to help build parts of my apps, and to automate repetitive tasks like resizing and exporting assets. For a designer who codes, an assistant that explains an error or drafts a function in seconds is a huge accelerator. I still read every line before it runs, and I test it.

Where AI doesn’t help (yet)

Strategy and judgement

AI can list options. It can’t decide which option is right for this client, with this budget, in this market. That requires understanding people, context and trade-offs, which is most of what a designer is actually paid for.

Logos and identity marks

I don’t use AI to generate logos. Generated marks tend to look generic, are hard to edit as clean vectors, can resemble existing marks without anyone noticing, and raise real questions about ownership. A logo has to be distinctive, ownable and built properly for every size. That still needs a designer and a construction grid, as I described in Brand Identity Is More Than a Logo.

Typography and fine detail

AI tools are still weak at typography: kerning, consistent letterforms, and especially Bangla script with its conjuncts and vowel signs. Any text in a generated image needs to be replaced with real, properly set type.

Knowing what’s true

Language models can state incorrect facts with complete confidence. In a design context, that means wrong statistics on an infographic, a made-up quote on a social post, or an inaccurate product claim. For anything factual, I verify.

My rules for using AI responsibly

  1. Client data stays private. I don’t paste confidential briefs, unreleased product details or personal data into tools without permission and without checking how the tool handles data.
  2. Generated images are drafts, not deliverables, unless the client has agreed and the tool’s licence clearly allows commercial use.
  3. No generated logos or identity marks.
  4. Every fact gets checked against a reliable source before it’s published.
  5. Be honest about AI use when it’s a meaningful part of the work, especially for imagery.
  6. Real people’s likenesses are off-limits for generated images unless they’ve agreed.
  7. The final decision is human. AI can propose; I decide, and I’m responsible for what goes out.

How my workflow looks now

A typical brand or campaign project now looks something like this:

  1. Brief: AI summarises the client’s messages; I correct and confirm.
  2. Research: AI helps me get oriented; I verify and dig deeper.
  3. Exploration: quick generated mood images and rough sketches for direction.
  4. Design: I build the real work by hand: identity, typography, layout and hierarchy.
  5. Production: AI-assisted editing for background extensions, clean-ups and resizing.
  6. Copy: AI drafts variations; I edit for tone, accuracy and Bangla.
  7. Review: I check every detail as if no AI was involved.

The time saved goes into the parts that matter most: thinking, crafting and talking to the people the work is for.

The skill that matters more now

If AI makes producing something easy, then the valuable skill is knowing whether that something is good. Taste, judgement, an understanding of design principles and the willingness to throw away a plausible but wrong idea are what separate a designer from a generator.

AI is a powerful assistant. It’s not the designer. In my work, it makes me faster at the parts I don’t enjoy, so I can spend more time on the parts that need a person.

Summary

  • Use AI for brainstorming, research summaries and repetitive production work.
  • Keep concept, taste and brand judgement human.
  • Check facts, rights and licences on everything AI produces.
  • Tell clients when and how AI was used.
  • Clear thinking and good briefs matter more now, not less.

item.title: Building a Personal Design System from One Colour
item.description: How one violet, one highlight colour and two typefaces became the rules behind my website, GitHub profile, CV and apps.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
Design systems are usually discussed as something big companies build: hundreds of components, a dedicated team, a documentation site. But the idea works at any size. Even a single designer benefits from a small set of rules that decide things once, so you don’t decide them again on every project.

Everything you see on this site, my GitHub profile, my CV and my app pages comes from one small system. It started from a single colour. This post explains how it’s built and why each rule exists.

Photo: Color Swatches by Tim Sullivan, CC0, via StockSnap.

Why bother with a system for one person

I work across very different surfaces: a portfolio website, a GitHub profile made of SVG cards, social posts, presentation decks, app interfaces, even broadcast graphics. Without a system, each one drifts. The violet gets slightly different, a new typeface sneaks in, buttons change shape.

A system gives three things:

  • Recognition. People start to associate a colour and a type pairing with your work.
  • Speed. You stop agonising over choices that were already made.
  • Consistency across tools. The same tokens can drive CSS, Figma styles and generated graphics.

Step 1: choose one base colour

My base is a deep violet, #3A10AD. I wanted something that felt confident and a little technical, stood apart from the usual corporate blues, and worked on both light and dark backgrounds.

From that one colour I built a full scale, from almost white to almost black:

Token Hex Typical use
brand-50 #F3F2FF Tinted backgrounds
brand-300 #B4ADFF Accents on dark backgrounds
brand-500 #6B4AFF Primary buttons, links, highlights
brand-900 #3A10AD The anchor colour
brand-950 #1E066F Deep backgrounds, dark sections

The steps in between fill in the gaps for hover states, borders and subtle fills. The key is that every violet anywhere in my work comes from this scale. No one-off purples.

Step 2: one highlight, used sparingly

Next to the violet sits Acid Lime, #D4FF24. It’s loud on purpose. The rule is that lime is a highlight only: one call-to-action button, a key word in a headline, an availability badge. Never a background for long text, never a second brand colour.

The scarcity is what makes it work. If everything is highlighted, nothing is. On this site, lime marks “Hire me”, the first name in the hero, and small status dots. Your eye goes to those things first, which is exactly where I want it.

Step 3: two typefaces with clear jobs

  • Sora for display and body text. It’s geometric and modern without feeling cold, and it reads well at small sizes.
  • JetBrains Mono for labels, tags, dates and anything technical. Monospace text signals “metadata” and gives the system a subtle engineering flavour that fits my background.

Two typefaces, two jobs. Headlines and paragraphs in Sora; eyebrows, chips and version numbers in JetBrains Mono. That’s the entire typography system, and it covers almost everything.

Step 4: check contrast with numbers, not eyes

A colour system isn’t finished until it passes accessibility checks. WCAG asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.

Some of the pairings in my system:

  • White text on brand-500 (#6B4AFF) is about 5.2:1, which is enough for button labels.
  • White on brand-900 (#3A10AD) is about 11.3:1.
  • Brand-950 (#1E066F) text on lime (#D4FF24) is about 13.8:1, so lime buttons use dark violet text.
  • Lime on white is only about 1.2:1, which is why lime never appears as text on a light background.

That last number is the reason for a rule that might otherwise feel arbitrary. Systems are full of rules like that: they look like taste, but they’re backed by measurements.

Step 5: turn decisions into tokens

The rules only become a system when they’re written down in a form tools can use. On this site, every colour is a CSS custom property:

:root {
  --brand-500: #6b4aff;
  --brand-900: #3a10ad;
  --lime: #d4ff24;
  --on-lime: #1e066f;
  --canvas: #ffffff;
  --ink: #160a45;
  --mark: var(--brand-600);
}

Components never use raw hex values. A button uses --brand-500, body text uses --ink, a highlight uses --lime. That indirection is what makes dark mode possible.

Step 6: light and dark from the same tokens

Dark mode isn’t a second design. It’s the same tokens pointing at different values. In dark mode, --canvas becomes a near-black violet, --ink becomes a soft off-white and --mark shifts from brand-600 to the lighter brand-300 so it stays readable. Components don’t change at all.

The same thinking applies outside the browser. The SVG cards on my GitHub profile come in light and dark versions generated by a small script, using the same token values and with the Sora and JetBrains Mono fonts embedded. GitHub shows the right one based on the viewer’s theme.

Step 7: a few components, not a library

My “component library” is small:

  • Buttons: primary (violet), highlight (lime), ghost and outline. Fully rounded.
  • Cards: a surface colour, a thin border, a 20px radius and a soft violet-tinted shadow.
  • Chips and tags: small, rounded, set in JetBrains Mono.
  • Section headers: a mono eyebrow, a divider line and a large Sora headline with one highlighted phrase.

Four or five patterns repeated consistently feel more designed than fifty patterns used once each.

Keep the system somewhere safe

I keep the full system, including tokens, type specimens, component notes and usage rules, as a single source of truth, separate from any one project. When I change a rule, I change it there first, then update the projects that use it. That stops the system from slowly forking into versions.

Start smaller than you think

If you want a personal design system, don’t start with components. Start with:

  1. One base colour and a tonal scale.
  2. One highlight colour with a strict rule for when it’s allowed.
  3. Two typefaces with clear jobs.
  4. Contrast checks for every text and background pair you use.
  5. Tokens so every tool reads the same values.

That’s enough to make everything you produce feel like it came from the same place. For how a system like this grows into a full brand for a client, see Brand Identity Is More Than a Logo.

Summary

  • Start with one base colour and one sparing highlight.
  • Give two typefaces clear, separate jobs.
  • Check contrast with numbers, not just your eyes.
  • Turn decisions into tokens shared by light and dark modes.
  • Build a few components, not a library, and keep it somewhere safe.

item.title: Making Alarms Reliable on Android: Lessons from Building TaskBell
item.description: Exact alarms, Doze, battery savers, reboots and time zones: what it takes for a reminder app to ring at the right second, every time.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
TaskBell has one job: ring before a task and ring again when it starts. A notes app can be a bit late. A reminder app that rings five minutes late is worse than no app at all, because you trusted it.

Getting an alarm to fire reliably on Android turned out to be the hardest part of the whole project. Android has spent years tightening what background apps are allowed to do, to protect battery life, and phone makers add their own aggressive battery savers on top. This post collects what I learned, in the hope it saves someone else a few weeks.

Photo: macro shot standard alarm clock, CC0, via rawpixel.

Pick the right kind of alarm

Android’s AlarmManager offers several ways to schedule work, and they are not equal.

  • Inexact alarms let the system batch your alarm with others to save battery. Fine for “sometime this hour”, useless for “at 4:45 PM”.
  • setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() fires at an exact time, even when the device is in Doze, the deep idle mode Android uses when a phone sits still with the screen off.
  • setAlarmClock() is meant for alarms the user sets and expects. The system treats it as the highest priority, shows the alarm icon in the status bar and lets the user see the next alarm.

For a reminder that the user explicitly asked for, setAlarmClock() is the most honest and most reliable choice. It tells the system, and the user, exactly what the app intends.

Permissions changed under my feet

Exact alarms are now permission-gated.

  • From Android 12, apps need the SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM permission to set exact alarms, and users can revoke it in settings.
  • Android 13 added USE_EXACT_ALARM, intended for apps whose core function is alarms or calendars. Google Play limits which apps may declare it.
  • From Android 14, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM is no longer granted by default to most newly installed apps targeting recent Android versions, so the app has to ask.

The practical lesson: never assume you have permission. Check with canScheduleExactAlarms() before scheduling, explain clearly why the permission matters, and send the user to the right settings screen if it’s missing.

Notifications have the same story. From Android 13, apps must request POST_NOTIFICATIONS at runtime. A reminder app without notification permission is silent, so TaskBell asks for it during setup with a plain explanation.

Ringing over the lock screen

When a task starts, TaskBell shows a full-screen alarm over the lock screen, the same way a clock app does. That uses a notification with a full-screen intent.

Android 14 tightened this too: full-screen intents are meant for calls and alarms, and users can turn the permission off. The app checks canUseFullScreenIntent() and falls back to a high-priority notification if it’s not allowed, rather than failing silently.

To ring even when the phone is on silent, the alarm sound uses alarm audio attributes (USAGE_ALARM). That plays on the alarm stream, which is controlled separately from the ringer, the same as a normal alarm clock. Users can still choose a softer pre-reminder and a louder start alarm, and High and Urgent tasks keep ringing until they’re answered.

Alarms are forgotten on reboot

Alarms registered with AlarmManager don’t survive a reboot. If your app doesn’t reschedule them, every reminder silently disappears the next time the phone restarts.

The fix is to treat the app’s own database as the source of truth and rebuild alarms from it whenever something might have cleared them:

  • After a reboot, with a receiver for BOOT_COMPLETED (and LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED if you want alarms to work before the user unlocks the phone for the first time).
  • After the app is updated, with MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED.
  • After the time or time zone changes, with TIME_SET and TIMEZONE_CHANGED, because a task at 9:00 AM should still ring at 9:00 AM local time after you travel or the clock is corrected.

The rescheduling code is the same function every time: read upcoming tasks, cancel anything stale, schedule the next alarms. Keeping it in one place means there’s only one thing to test.

Missed alarms should be visible

Even with everything done right, alarms can be missed: the phone was off, the battery died, a manufacturer’s battery saver killed the app. When that happens, the worst outcome is silence.

TaskBell keeps a Missed list. On startup and after a reboot, it checks for tasks whose alarm time passed without firing and shows them clearly, so the user at least knows what they missed.

The real enemy: OEM battery savers

Stock Android behaves well if you follow the rules. Many phones don’t run stock Android. Several manufacturers add their own background-killing features, battery “optimisers” and auto-start blockers. These can stop alarms or kill the app in ways that the official APIs can’t detect.

There’s no code-only fix for this. What works is honesty and guidance:

  • An alarm health check. TaskBell has a screen that checks the settings that affect reliability (notification permission, exact alarm permission, full-screen alerts, battery optimisation) and shows which ones need attention.
  • Direct links to settings. Where Android allows it, the app opens the exact settings page instead of describing a path through menus.
  • A test alarm. Setup ends with a test alarm, so the user hears it working before relying on it.

The community site Don’t Kill My App documents manufacturer-specific battery behaviour and is worth reading if you build anything that runs in the background.

Design matters as much as code

Most reliability problems end up in front of the user, so the interface carries a lot of the weight.

  • Confirm what will happen. After saving a task, TaskBell shows “Alarms set: 4:45 PM and 5:00 PM”, so the user knows exactly when to expect it.
  • Explain permissions in plain words, with the reason first and the button second.
  • Make setup short. Three steps and a test alarm is about as much as people will do.
  • Never fail silently. If the app can’t guarantee an alarm, say so.

A checklist if you’re building something similar

  1. Use setAlarmClock() for user-facing alarms.
  2. Check exact-alarm, notification and full-screen permissions every time, not just at install.
  3. Store tasks in a local database and treat it as the source of truth.
  4. Reschedule after boot, app updates, and time or time-zone changes.
  5. Use alarm audio attributes so alarms ring in silent mode.
  6. Track and show missed alarms.
  7. Add a health check and a test alarm for phones with aggressive battery savers.

Building TaskBell taught me that reliability is a feature you design, not just a bug you fix. You can read more about the app on its page: TaskBell.

Summary

  • Use the right exact-alarm API for the job.
  • Ask for permissions clearly and handle changes.
  • Ring over the lock screen with a full-screen intent.
  • Reschedule alarms after reboot and show missed ones.
  • Guide users past aggressive OEM battery savers.

item.title: Designing Bilingual Brands: Setting Bangla and English Together
item.description: Why Bangla and English type rarely match out of the box, and the practical rules I use to make them feel like one brand.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
Most brands in Bangladesh speak two languages. The logo might be in English, the Facebook posts in Bangla, the event banner in both. Yet in many identities the Bangla side is an afterthought: a default font dropped in at the last minute, sitting awkwardly next to a carefully chosen English typeface.

When Bangla and English are designed together, the brand feels confident and local. When they aren’t, it looks like two brands sharing a page. These are the rules I follow to make them work as one.

Photo: Typography Letter by Raphael Schaller, CC0, via StockSnap.

Why the two scripts don’t match by default

Latin and Bangla are built on different structures, and you can see it the moment you put them side by side.

  • Different anchor lines. Latin letters sit on a baseline. Bangla letters hang from a headline, the horizontal stroke called the matra that runs along the top of most letters.
  • Different vertical extent. Bangla has vowel signs that sit above the headline and below the letters, and conjuncts (যুক্তবর্ণ) can stack consonants vertically. A line of Bangla needs more vertical room than a line of English.
  • Different apparent size. At the same point size, Bangla often looks smaller than Latin text, because much of its height is taken up by marks above and below the main letters.
  • Different stroke logic. Many Latin typefaces are geometric or humanist; Bangla typefaces have their own traditions, from calligraphic to modern geometric. A perfect match rarely exists.

So “use the same size and spacing for both” almost never works.

Rule 1: pick typefaces as a pair

I choose the Bangla and English typefaces together, looking for shared qualities rather than identical shapes:

  • Similar stroke contrast. A low-contrast, even-stroke Latin typeface pairs better with a low-contrast Bangla one.
  • Similar weight range. If headlines use a bold weight in English, the Bangla typeface needs a genuinely bold weight too, not a faked one.
  • Similar personality. Rounded and friendly with rounded and friendly; sharp and technical with sharp and technical.

Some typeface families are designed for both scripts, such as Noto Sans and Noto Sans Bengali or Hind and Hind Siliguri, which makes matching much easier. For more distinctive brands, I pair a characterful English typeface with the Bangla face whose rhythm feels closest, then adjust size and spacing by eye.

Rule 2: always use Unicode fonts

Many people in Bangladesh learned to type Bangla with Bijoy, and older documents often use ANSI fonts such as SutonnyMJ, where Bangla letters are mapped onto Latin character codes. Those files look right on the designer’s computer but break everywhere else: text turns into Latin gibberish when the font is missing, can’t be searched, and won’t survive being pasted into a website or app.

For anything digital, I insist on Unicode Bangla fonts. Text stays readable on every device, works with screen readers and search engines, and can be copied, translated and indexed. (I built a small Bijoy typing practice page for people learning the layout, but the text it produces should still end up in Unicode.)

Rule 3: match apparent size, not point size

When Bangla and English sit next to each other, as in a bilingual headline or a logo with both names, I adjust sizes until they look equal. In practice that often means setting the Bangla a little larger than the English, then checking by eye at the final size.

The test is simple: squint. If one language jumps out as bigger or heavier, adjust until neither dominates (unless one is meant to).

Rule 4: give Bangla more line height

Line height that looks comfortable for English can make Bangla feel cramped, and in tight layouts it can even clip vowel signs above or below the line. I set Bangla body text with more generous line height than English, and I test the tallest conjuncts and the deepest marks in the real typeface, not just a sample sentence.

In apps this matters even more. A button or list row with a fixed height that fits English may cut off Bangla. I design components to grow with their text instead of fixing heights to the English version, as I described in Building Offline-First Apps for Bangladesh.

Rule 5: align to what each script respects

In a bilingual logo or lockup, I have to decide which lines to align. Aligning the English baseline with the bottom of the Bangla letters can look fine; aligning the top of the English capitals with the Bangla headline often looks even better, because the matra creates a strong visual line.

There’s no universal answer. I try both alignments, look at them at the size they’ll be used, and pick the one where the two names read as one unit.

Rule 6: decide the hierarchy

When both languages appear, one usually leads. For a local community organisation, Bangla might lead and English support. For a tech company working with international partners, the reverse. Making this decision explicit, and writing it into the brand guidelines, prevents every new banner from reinventing it.

Common patterns I use:

  • Bangla primary, English secondary: the Bangla name larger, the English name smaller underneath.
  • Equal weight: both names at matched apparent size, separated by a clear divider or placed side by side.
  • Context switch: Bangla for local social media, English for international documents, with the same layout system for both.

Rule 7: numbers, dates and punctuation

Bilingual brands also need rules for the small stuff:

  • Digits: use Bangla digits (০–৯) in Bangla text and Latin digits in English text, consistently.
  • Dates: decide whether Bangla materials use the Bangla calendar, the Gregorian calendar, or both.
  • Punctuation: Bangla uses the দাঁড়ি (।) as its full stop. It’s a small detail, but getting it wrong is noticeable to every native reader.
  • Currency: ৳ for taka, with consistent spacing and grouping.

Rule 8: put it in the guidelines

All of this disappears if it lives only in my head. A bilingual brand guideline should include:

  • the Bangla and English typefaces, with weights for each role
  • the size relationship between them (for example, “Bangla headlines one step larger”)
  • line height for each script
  • examples of correct bilingual lockups and headlines
  • digit, date and punctuation rules

I treat this as part of the brand identity process I described in Brand Identity Is More Than a Logo.

Designing for the audience you actually have

Treating Bangla as a first-class part of a brand isn’t just good typography. It’s respect for the people the brand is speaking to. Most of them read Bangla first. A brand that clearly took the time to get Bangla right earns trust that an English-only identity, or a careless translation, never will.

Summary

  • Choose Bangla and Latin typefaces as a pair.
  • Always use Unicode Bangla fonts for anything digital.
  • Match apparent size and give Bangla more line height.
  • Decide which script leads, and handle numbers and dates.
  • Write all of it into the brand guidelines.

item.title: Moving from SDI to IP Workflows (SMPTE ST 2110): Planning, Risks and a Phased Migration Roadmap for Bangladesh
item.description: Planning a move from SDI to SMPTE ST 2110 IP workflows: what changes, PTP timing, network design, risks for Bangladeshi TV channels and a phased roadmap.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
Walk into almost any TV station in Dhaka and you will find the same thing behind the racks: thick bundles of coaxial cable, BNC connectors and a large SDI router at the centre of everything. It is reliable, it is familiar, and the engineers who built it know every path by heart.

The rest of the broadcast world is slowly replacing that cable with network switches, fibre and software, mostly built on a family of standards called SMPTE ST 2110. The question for Bangladeshi channels is not whether IP arrives, but when, how fast and in what order, because our budgets, our power supply, our import process and our skills market are different from those of a broadcaster in London or Montreal.

I work in a Master Control Room at Channel i, so this post looks at the move from the inside: what changes, what can go wrong, and a phased roadmap that keeps the on-air signal safe the whole way through.

Photo: , CC0, via rawpixel.

Where Bangladeshi broadcasting stands today

Bangladesh has around three dozen television channels on air, the state broadcaster BTV plus a large group of private satellite channels, most of them headquartered within a few kilometres of each other in Dhaka. Many of these facilities were designed between the mid-2000s and the mid-2010s, when the industry moved from tape to file-based workflows and from SD towards HD.

A typical Bangladeshi facility today looks like this:

  • An SDI core. HD-SDI (or 3G-SDI) routing, with some SD still in archives and older equipment.
  • File-based ingest and playout, driven by automation, with news and programmes on shared storage.
  • Satellite uplink for the main channel, including on the country’s own communications satellite launched in 2018, plus a teleport or backup path.
  • Many distribution routes at once: cable operators, DTH, IPTV, and a growing share of viewers on YouTube, Facebook and channel apps.
  • Field contribution over the internet, using bonded cellular units and streaming protocols, because district bureaus and live events rarely have dedicated fibre.

So in practice our channels are already half on IP at the edges. What is still SDI is the core: the router, the production switchers, the master control chain and the cables between them. That core is what ST 2110 replaces.

SDI and ST 2110 in one minute

SDI carries uncompressed video, embedded audio and data down one coaxial cable, point to point, with almost no delay. HD-SDI runs at about 1.5 Gb/s, 3G-SDI at about 3 Gb/s and 12G-SDI at about 12 Gb/s for UHD. It is simple and deterministic. Its weakness is that every new connection needs a physical cable and a router port, and every format upgrade tends to mean new hardware.

ST 2110 sends the same professional signals over a managed IP network, but splits them into separate streams (“essences”):

  • ST 2110-20: uncompressed video
  • ST 2110-30: uncompressed audio (based on AES67)
  • ST 2110-40: ancillary data such as captions and timecode
  • ST 2110-22: compressed video (for example JPEG XS) where bandwidth matters
  • ST 2110-21: rules for how evenly packets are sent

Around it sit three things every engineer has to learn:

  • Timing with PTP. Devices agree on time using the Precision Time Protocol, under the broadcast profile in SMPTE ST 2059. A GPS-locked grandmaster replaces the old reference generator. Timing stops being a cable and becomes a network service.
  • Redundancy with ST 2022-7. Each stream is sent twice over two separate networks (“red” and “blue”), and receivers rebuild a clean signal from whichever packets arrive. It is the IP version of the main and backup chains every MCR already runs, which I described in Inside a Master Control Room.
  • Control with AMWA NMOS. IS-04 lets devices announce themselves and IS-05 connects senders to receivers, so a control system can behave like the router panel operators already know.

Why a Bangladeshi channel would move at all

IP should never be adopted because it is fashionable. In our market the real drivers are:

  1. End-of-life SDI cores. Routers, switchers and frame-sync cards bought around 2010 to 2015 are reaching the end of vendor support. When a core has to be replaced anyway, buying IP-ready equipment avoids paying twice.
  2. HD everywhere, and UHD later. Upgrading formats on IP is mostly about bandwidth and licences, not rewiring the building.
  3. Remote and distributed production. Cricket, elections, Ekushey February, Eid programming and big talk shows increasingly mix studios, outside locations and remote guests. IP makes it easier to share sources between studios, control rooms and even other buildings.
  4. Digital-first distribution. When a large part of the audience watches on YouTube, Facebook and apps, the facility needs to feed many outputs at once. Software-based playout and graphics fit naturally on an IP plant.
  5. A local skills advantage. Bangladesh has a deep pool of networking talent from its ISPs, telecom operators and IT sector. Routing, switching and multicast are skills we can hire and grow locally.

Planning: what to settle before buying anything

1. Write down why. One page: what problem the move solves, what success looks like, and what must never happen (usually: never lose the on-air signal).

2. Inventory the plant. List every SDI source, destination, format, frame rate and audio map. Mark what is end-of-life, what is new and what can stay SDI for years with a gateway.

3. Decide the architecture early. Two common network designs exist: a large central switch, or a spine-and-leaf fabric that scales by adding switches. For most Bangladeshi channels, a modest spine-leaf design with fully separate red and blue networks is a sensible default.

4. Do the bandwidth sums. One uncompressed 1080p50 or 1080i stream is roughly 1.5 to 3 Gb/s. Multiply by sources, then add headroom, then double it for 2022-7 redundancy. Link speeds, switch buffers and optics follow from this, not from a brochure.

5. Choose standards over brands. Insist on ST 2110, ST 2059 PTP, ST 2022-7 and NMOS IS-04/IS-05, and ask vendors for proof of interoperability, such as participation in the JT-NM Tested programme. Avoid any design that only works with one manufacturer’s controller.

6. Count the full cost, in taka. Budget for switches, optics, PTP grandmasters, gateways, a broadcast controller, monitoring, training, spares held locally, UPS and cooling, not just the headline devices. Most equipment is priced in US dollars and imported, so exchange-rate movement and import timelines belong in the plan from day one.

7. Plan for people. Who will run the network at 3 a.m.? Broadcast and IT staff need to become one team, with shared on-call rules and the same checklists and handovers the MCR already depends on.

The risks, and how to manage them

Risk What it looks like in Bangladesh How to reduce it
Timing (PTP) failure Lip-sync drift, devices that won’t lock, glitches nobody can explain Two GPS-locked grandmasters, PTP-aware switches, timing alarms in the MCR, a simple PTP runbook
Network misconfiguration A multicast flood or wrong IGMP setting takes down many feeds at once Change control, a test lab, configuration backups, strict separation of red and blue networks
Interoperability gaps A camera, switcher and controller from three vendors don’t agree Standards-based tenders, JT-NM-tested kit, a proof-of-concept before the main order
Skills gap SDI veterans and IT staff speak different languages Joint training, a small lab to practise on, pair broadcast and network engineers
Import and currency delays Equipment held up by letters of credit, dollar shortages or customs; prices rise mid-project Order critical items early, phase purchases, keep local spares, fix prices where possible
Power and heat Load-shedding, generator switchover glitches, hot and humid equipment rooms Double-conversion UPS on all network gear, dual power supplies, proper cooling and dust control
Cyber security A networked plant can be reached from places a coaxial cable never could Segmented networks, no direct internet on media networks, access control, logging
On-air disruption during cutover A migration step goes wrong live Never cut over the main chain first; keep SDI fallback paths and rehearse rollback

A phased roadmap that keeps the channel on air

The safest migrations do not replace everything at once. They grow IP from the edges inward, with a working SDI fallback at every step. The durations below are typical for a mid-sized channel and will vary with budget and import timelines.

Phase 0: Readiness (3 to 6 months)

  • Train a core team in multicast, IGMP, PTP and ST 2110 basics.
  • Build a small lab: two switches, a PTP grandmaster, a few gateways and a monitoring tool.
  • Complete the inventory, the architecture and the risk register.
  • Exit when: the team can build, break and fix a small 2110 network in the lab.

Phase 1: IP at the edges (6 to 12 months)

  • Move audio first with AES67-compatible equipment. It teaches the same ideas (PTP, multicast, discovery) at a fraction of the bandwidth and risk.
  • Standardise field contribution on streaming protocols such as SRT for remote bureaus and events.
  • Use IP for non-critical paths such as monitoring feeds and multiviewers.
  • Exit when: IP audio and contribution run daily without incidents.

Phase 2: The first IP island (12 to 18 months)

  • Build one new studio or production control room natively on ST 2110, with gateways to the existing SDI core.
  • Install red and blue networks, redundant PTP, an NMOS-based broadcast controller and network monitoring.
  • Operate the island under real production pressure while the SDI core stays untouched.
  • Exit when: the island has run real shows for months with documented fault handling.

Phase 3: Core and master control (18 to 30 months)

  • Replace the SDI router with the IP fabric, moving sources across in planned windows.
  • Migrate master control and playout last, with an SDI or tested backup chain kept ready for rollback.
  • Update every MCR procedure, alarm and handover note for the new plant.
  • Exit when: the main and backup chains both run on IP and failover has been rehearsed.

Phase 4: Optimise and grow (ongoing)

  • Move more processing into software: graphics, multiviewers, playout.
  • Extend remote production between studios, bureaus and venues.
  • Prepare for UHD or higher frame rates where the business case exists.

Many Bangladeshi channels will reasonably stay hybrid for years: SDI where it still works well, IP where it clearly helps, and gateways in between. That is not failing to modernise. It is good engineering under real constraints.

What the rest of the world teaches us

We don’t have to learn every lesson ourselves:

  • BBC Cymru Wales opened its Central Square headquarters in Cardiff in 2020, widely cited as one of the first large broadcast centres built around ST 2110. Its main lesson for others has been how much effort goes into integration, timing and testing compared with simply buying equipment.
  • CBC/Radio-Canada moved into its new Montreal headquarters around the same time, also designed as a large IP facility, showing that a public broadcaster can migrate a whole building while staying on air.
  • The EBU (European Broadcasting Union) publishes guidance for broadcasters, including its Technology Pyramid for Media Nodes (EBU Tech 3371), which helps buyers specify the minimum capabilities IP equipment should have.
  • The JT-NM Tested programme checks how well products from different vendors follow ST 2110, PTP and NMOS. Its reports are a useful filter before writing a tender.
  • AMWA maintains the NMOS specifications as open, free documents, so any engineer in Dhaka can read exactly what a controller is supposed to do.

The common thread is consistent: successful broadcasters treated IP migration as a change in people and processes as much as in technology, and they kept a safe path to air throughout.

Where a Bangladeshi engineer should start

  1. Learn networking properly. Multicast and IGMP are the heart of ST 2110. Our ISP and telecom sector is full of people who can teach this.
  2. Understand PTP. Most IP plant problems eventually lead back to timing.
  3. Practise with audio. AES67 equipment is affordable and teaches the same concepts.
  4. Read the standards summaries. SMPTE ST 2110 parts, ST 2059 and NMOS IS-04/IS-05. Know what each does.
  5. Bring the MCR mindset with you. Signal paths, redundancy, checklists and rehearsed failover matter even more on IP.

The coaxial cable on the desk is going away, slowly. The job isn’t. It is still about getting a clean picture from one place to another, on time, without the viewer ever noticing, whether that viewer is in Dhaka, in a district town, or watching a Bangladeshi channel on a phone halfway around the world.

Summary

  • Most Bangladeshi channels still run on SDI, and that’s fine for now.
  • ST 2110 sends video, audio and data as separate IP streams.
  • Settle timing, networking and skills before buying.
  • Move in phases: edges first, the on-air core last.
  • Learn from others and start building IP skills now.

item.title: Brand Identity Is More Than a Logo: A Practical Process for Small Organisations
item.description: The step-by-step process I use with startups, youth organisations and shops to go from a vague brief to an identity people can actually use.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
When a small organisation asks for “a logo”, they almost always need more than one. They need a way to look consistent across a Facebook page, a banner at an event, a business card and a pitch deck, usually made by different people with different tools.

That’s what a brand identity is: not a single mark, but a system that lets anyone produce something that clearly belongs to the same organisation. Over the years I’ve designed identities for youth organisations, tech communities, fashion labels and retailers. This is the process I use, scaled for teams that don’t have a marketing department.

Photo: Designer Logo by Messala Ciulla, CC0, via StockSnap.

1. Start with questions, not sketches

The most expensive mistake in branding is designing before you understand the problem. Before I open Illustrator, I want answers to a short list of questions:

  • Who is this for? Not “everyone”. The two or three groups whose opinion really matters.
  • What should they feel? Three or four words, such as “trustworthy, modern, local”, work better than a paragraph.
  • What makes you different? If you swapped your name with a competitor’s, what would be wrong?
  • Where will the brand live? Social media, signage, packaging, uniforms, an app? This decides which formats matter most.
  • What exists already? Old logos, colours people already associate with you, things the team loves or hates.

I write the answers up as a one-page brief and get the client to agree to it. Later, when opinions clash, the brief is the referee.

2. Research the space

Next I look at the people the brand will stand next to: competitors, similar organisations, and the visual habits of the sector. If every education initiative uses blue and a graduation cap, a new one can either fit the category deliberately or stand out deliberately. Both are valid, as long as the choice is conscious.

I collect references into a single board and mark what to avoid as clearly as what to aim for. Clients often find the “avoid” list more useful.

3. Concept before polish

I sketch broadly before committing to anything. A good logo usually comes from one clear idea: a letterform, a symbol tied to what the organisation does, or a shape that captures its personality.

I usually present two or three distinct directions, not ten variations of the same one. Each direction gets a short rationale explaining the idea behind it. Clients choose better when they’re comparing ideas rather than shades of the same shape.

4. Build the mark properly

Once a direction is chosen, the craft begins:

  • Construction. I rebuild the mark on a grid so curves, angles and spacing are consistent. Construction grids aren’t decoration; they make the mark feel intentional and easier to redraw.
  • Small sizes. The logo must work as a 32-pixel favicon and a social profile picture, so I test it tiny early and simplify details that disappear.
  • One colour. It must work in solid black, solid white and a single brand colour, for stamps, embroidery, engraving and photocopies.
  • Variations. A full lockup with the name, a compact version, and an icon-only mark for tight spaces.

5. Colour and type, chosen as a system

A logo alone doesn’t make an identity. Colour and typography do most of the everyday work.

Colour. I pick a primary colour, a supporting palette and usually one accent. Then I check contrast so text stays readable (WCAG’s 4.5:1 for normal text is a good baseline), and I define exact values for screen (HEX and RGB) and print (CMYK, and Pantone where it matters). Print colours can look very different from screen colours, so I always check a printed proof when the budget allows. I describe how I build a colour scale in more detail in Building a Personal Design System from One Colour.

Typography. I choose one or two typefaces with clear roles: one for headlines, one for body text. For organisations in Bangladesh, the Bangla typeface needs as much attention as the English one, and the two have to feel like they belong together. I wrote about that in Designing Bilingual Brands.

6. Show it in use

A logo on a white artboard tells you almost nothing. Before handover, I show the identity applied to the places it will actually live:

  • social media post templates and profile images
  • an event banner or standee
  • business cards, letterheads and envelopes
  • a presentation title slide
  • merchandise like T-shirts, if the organisation uses them

Mock-ups catch real problems: a tagline too long for a banner, a colour that vibrates on screen, a logo that disappears on a busy photo.

7. Write guidelines people will read

Brand guidelines fail when they’re 60 pages nobody opens. For small organisations, I aim for something short and practical:

  • The logo: versions, minimum size, clear space, and a page of “don’ts” (no stretching, no recolouring, no drop shadows).
  • Colours: exact values for screen and print, with examples of good combinations.
  • Typography: which typefaces to use for what, with sizes for common formats.
  • Templates: ready-to-edit files for the things the team makes most often.

Templates matter more than rules. A volunteer with ten minutes before an event will use a ready social post template; they won’t read a rulebook.

8. Hand over files that work

The final package should let the client work without coming back to me for every small job:

  • logos in SVG, PDF and high-resolution PNG, in full colour, black and white
  • colour values in one easy-to-copy document
  • font names and where to get them
  • editable templates (Figma, Illustrator, PowerPoint or Canva, depending on what the team uses)
  • the guidelines as a PDF

I organise them in clearly named folders. “Logo_final_FINAL2.png” has no place in a brand handover.

Common mistakes I see

  • Starting with “make it pop”. Without a brief, feedback becomes personal taste.
  • Too many colours. Most small brands need one main colour, one or two supporting colours and neutrals.
  • A logo that only works big. If it fails at profile-picture size, it fails where most people will see it.
  • No templates. Without them, every new post becomes a fresh design, and the brand drifts within months.
  • Ignoring the second language. A beautiful English wordmark paired with a default Bangla font looks unfinished.

Brand is what people do with it

The identity I hand over is only the beginning. A brand becomes real when the team uses it consistently, week after week, on every post and every banner. My job is to make that easy: a clear idea, a solid system, and tools simple enough that people actually use them.

Summary

  • Start with questions and a clear brief, not sketches.
  • Research the space before drawing concepts.
  • Choose a concept before polishing it.
  • Build colour and type as a system, and show it in real use.
  • Hand over readable guidelines and files that work.

item.title: Design Theory You Can Use Tomorrow: Gestalt, Hierarchy and Simple Research
item.description: The handful of design principles and research methods I actually use every week, explained without the jargon.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
There’s a gap between design theory as it’s taught and design as it’s practised. Theory can feel abstract: lists of principles, laws named after psychologists, diagrams of eyes scanning pages. Practice is a deadline and a client asking why the poster “doesn’t feel right”.

The good news is that a small amount of theory goes a long way. These are the principles and research methods I actually reach for, with examples of how each one changes a real design.

Photo: Seymour Chwast lights Tyler! design by libraryofcongress, CC0, via rawpixel.

Gestalt: how people group what they see

Gestalt psychology describes how our brains organise visual information into groups and wholes. You don’t need to memorise every principle, but five of them explain most layout problems.

Proximity

Things that are close together are seen as related. This is the single most useful principle in layout. If a caption is the same distance from the image above it and the paragraph below it, readers can’t tell which one it belongs to. Tighten the space to what it belongs to, loosen the space to everything else.

In practice: on event posters, group the date, time and venue tightly into one block, separated clearly from the speaker names. People will read it as “the details” at a glance.

Similarity

Things that look alike are seen as the same kind of thing. Consistent colour, shape or style signals a category. That’s why all buttons in a system should look like buttons, and why a link styled differently on one page confuses people.

Common region

Things inside the same boundary, such as a card, a box or a background colour, are seen as a group, even if they’re not especially close. Cards work because of common region.

Closure and continuity

We complete incomplete shapes and follow smooth lines. Logo designers use closure all the time, letting the viewer fill in a missing piece of a letter or symbol. Continuity explains why aligned edges feel calm: the eye travels along them.

Figure and ground

We separate what’s in front (figure) from what’s behind (ground). When figure and ground compete, as with text over a busy photo, the design feels noisy. A darkened overlay, a solid band or simply a calmer image restores the separation.

Visual hierarchy: deciding what’s seen first

Every layout answers the question “what should people notice first, second and third?” If you don’t answer it deliberately, the layout answers it for you, usually badly.

The tools of hierarchy are simple:

  • Size: bigger is seen first.
  • Contrast: high-contrast elements stand out against low-contrast ones.
  • Colour: a single accent colour draws the eye. This is why my own design system allows only one highlight colour, Acid Lime, and uses it sparingly.
  • Position: in left-to-right languages, people tend to start top-left.
  • Space: an element surrounded by empty space feels important.

A quick check: blur your design (or step back and squint). The shapes you still see are your hierarchy. If the most important message isn’t among them, the design needs work.

A few useful “laws”

Two more principles are worth knowing because they turn directly into design decisions.

Fitts’s law says the time to reach a target depends on its size and distance. On a phone, that means primary actions should be large and easy to reach with a thumb. It’s why the main buttons on this site stretch to full width on phones.

Hick’s law says decision time grows with the number of choices. Long menus and crowded dashboards slow people down. Grouping related items, for example putting experience, awards and tools under one “About” menu, keeps the main navigation short and easy to scan.

These aren’t rules to obey blindly, but they’re good arguments when you need to explain a design decision to a client.

Research doesn’t have to be expensive

Theory tells you how people tend to see things. Research tells you how your audience actually behaves. Many designers skip research because it sounds slow and costly. Most of the useful methods are neither.

The five-second test

Show someone a design for five seconds, then hide it and ask: what was this about? What do you remember? Who is it for? It’s a fast way to check whether a poster, landing page or social post communicates its main message. If people can’t tell you the event name after five seconds, the hierarchy needs fixing.

Quick usability tests

Give a few people a realistic task (“record a 500 taka expense from bKash”) and watch them try it without helping. Jakob Nielsen’s well-known argument is that testing with around five users reveals most of the major usability problems in a design, and that several small rounds beat one big study. In my experience, the first two or three people already reveal the problems that matter most.

Tips that make it work:

  • Ask people to think out loud.
  • Don’t explain the interface; watch where they hesitate.
  • Write down what they do, not just what they say.

Surveys, used carefully

Surveys are good for understanding patterns across many people and bad for understanding why. I co-authored a study on public reactions to the November 2025 earthquake in Bangladesh, based on 110 survey responses, and the experience taught me how much the wording of each question shapes the answers. Keep questions neutral, avoid asking two things at once, and pilot the survey with a few people before sending it widely.

Interviews

Short conversations with real users, focused on their past behaviour (“tell me about the last time you tracked your spending”) rather than hypotheticals (“would you use an app that…?”), reveal motivations and context that no survey will.

Card sorting

For navigation and information architecture, give people cards with your content topics and ask them to group them in ways that make sense. It shows you how your audience expects things to be organised, which is often different from how your team thinks about them.

Putting theory and research together

A typical project for me looks like this:

  1. Brief and questions to understand what success means.
  2. Quick research such as a few interviews, a look at competitors, maybe a short survey.
  3. Design using principles: Gestalt for grouping, hierarchy for emphasis, Fitts and Hick for interaction.
  4. Test early with a five-second test or a small usability session on a rough version.
  5. Revise and test again before polishing.

Theory gives you a starting point that’s probably right. Research tells you where it’s wrong for these particular people. Together, they turn “I think this looks good” into “this works, and here’s why”.

Summary

  • Gestalt explains how people group what they see.
  • Decide what should be seen first, second and third.
  • Hick’s and Fitts’s laws help make choices quick and targets easy.
  • Five quick user tests find most usability problems.
  • Combine theory with simple research before big decisions.

Further reading

If you want to go deeper, the classic starting points are Don Norman’s The Design of Everyday Things for how people understand objects and interfaces, and Steve Krug’s Don’t Make Me Think for practical, low-cost usability testing. Both are short, readable and still relevant decades after they were first published.

item.title: Building Offline-First Apps for Bangladesh
item.description: Why my apps work without the internet, keep data on the phone and speak Bangla first, and the design and engineering choices that follow.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
Every app I’ve released has the same three rules: it works without the internet, the user’s data stays on their phone, and it treats Bangla as a first-class language rather than a translation added at the end.

None of these rules came from a design principle I read somewhere. They came from watching how people around me actually use their phones. This post explains why I build this way and what it changes in the design and the code, using two of my apps as examples: Taka, a personal finance manager, and TaskBell, a task manager with alarm reminders.

Photo: Iphone Smartphone by Adrianna Calvo, CC0, via StockSnap.

Why offline-first

“Offline-first” means the app is designed to work fully without a network connection. Syncing or online features, if they exist at all, are extras on top of an app that already works.

For many users in Bangladesh, that matters for practical reasons:

  • Connectivity is uneven. Mobile data can be slow or patchy outside city centres, inside buildings, or during busy times.
  • Data costs money. People are careful about what eats their data pack.
  • Phones are shared and storage is tight. Many users run budget Android phones with little free space, so a light app that doesn’t download content constantly is easier to keep.
  • Trust is low for apps that ask for accounts. A money app that wants your phone number, email and a sign-up before you can record your first expense loses people at the first screen.

An app that opens instantly, works in a basement and doesn’t ask for an account removes all of those problems at once.

Privacy as a feature, not a policy page

Both Taka and TaskBell keep data on the device. TaskBell goes further and doesn’t request the internet permission at all, which means it physically can’t send your tasks anywhere. There’s no account, no ads and no analytics.

This is a design decision as much as an engineering one. When an app records your savings, loans and bKash balance, or your private reminders and contacts, the safest data is data that never leaves the phone. It also makes the app much simpler to build and maintain. There’s no server to pay for, no database to secure, and no breach to apologise for.

The trade-off is that the user becomes responsible for their own backup. So backup has to be easy. In TaskBell, a single backup file is saved to a folder the user chooses, and restoring shows a preview of what’s inside before anything is overwritten. In Taka, the same idea applies: the user owns the file and decides where it goes.

Designing for Bangla first

Supporting Bangla is not just translating strings. It affects layout, typography and even the words you choose.

  • Text length changes. A button label that fits in English may wrap in Bangla, or the other way round. I design layouts that can grow instead of fixing widths to the English text.
  • Script needs room. Bangla letters have marks above and below the main line, and conjuncts can be tall. Line height that looks fine for English can clip Bangla.
  • Numbers matter. In a finance app, people expect to see Bangla digits (০১২৩…) when they choose Bangla, and amounts in the local grouping style. Taka handles amounts like ৳3,46,064.75 rather than forcing Western grouping.
  • Words should be familiar. Financial terms like DPS, Sanchayapatra and FDR are what people actually say. Using the everyday term is better than a literal translation nobody uses.

I go deeper into setting Bangla and English together in Designing Bilingual Brands.

Building for the local context

Offline-first also means thinking about what people actually need to track. Taka isn’t a generic budgeting app with a Bangladeshi flag on it. It handles cash, bKash, Nagad, bank accounts, DPS, Sanchayapatra, loans given and taken, and insurance, because that’s what a household’s money really looks like here.

The lesson generalises: the more specific your app is to the people using it, the less it needs to explain itself.

The engineering choices that follow

Once you commit to offline-first, several technical decisions become obvious.

The local database is the source of truth. Everything the user sees comes from a database on the device. Screens read from it, actions write to it, and nothing waits on a network request.

Every write must be safe. If the phone dies mid-save, the data must still be consistent. That means transactions for anything that touches more than one record, and careful migrations when the database structure changes between versions.

Migrations need testing. Users can skip versions. A user going from version 0.2 to 0.9 has to land on the correct database schema without losing anything. I keep migrations small and test upgrades from older versions, not just fresh installs.

Background work has to respect the OS. TaskBell’s whole purpose is to ring at the right time, so it has to work with Android’s alarm and battery rules rather than against them. That deserves its own post: Making Alarms Reliable on Android.

Updates still need a channel. Without an app store or a server, users still need to find out about new versions. My apps are distributed as APKs from GitHub Releases, with a simple update check and a release page that explains what changed. TaskBell’s site and Taka’s site both live on this domain.

The tools

I’ve used different stacks for different apps. Taka is built with Flutter, which made it practical to design a polished, consistent interface and handle Bangla and English from a single codebase. TaskBell is written in Kotlin as a native Android app, because alarms, notifications and lock-screen behaviour are deeply tied to Android itself, and native code gives the most control over them.

The choice of framework matters less than the principles. If the app works offline, stores data locally and is built for the language and context of its users, the framework is just the way you get there.

What I’d tell someone starting out

  1. Decide early what must work offline. Usually the answer is “everything the user does every day”.
  2. Treat privacy as a product feature. Fewer permissions and no account are selling points, so say so clearly.
  3. Design for Bangla from the first sketch, not after the English version is finished.
  4. Make backup and restore boring and safe. If users own their data, they need an easy way to protect it.
  5. Test on cheap phones. If it runs well on a budget device, it runs well everywhere.

Building this way is slower at the start, but it produces apps that people can trust on the first day and keep using for years.

Summary

  • Design apps to work with no signal first.
  • Keep data on the device: privacy as a feature.
  • Design for Bangla first, not as a translation.
  • Respect budget phones, data packs and local habits.
  • Keep the engineering simple and the app light.

item.title: Leading Volunteer Creative Teams: What Student Organisations Taught Me
item.description: Lessons from leading design teams and events in student and youth organisations, where nobody is paid and everyone is busy.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Fahim
item.content:encoded:
Leading a team of paid professionals is hard. Leading a team of volunteers is a different kind of hard. Nobody has to show up. Everyone has exams, jobs or family commitments that rightly come first. The only thing holding the team together is that people want to be there.

Most of my leadership experience comes from exactly that setting. I led the branding and communication team at NUSDF Bangladesh (the National University Skill Development Forum), served as General Secretary of the IEEE ISTT Student Branch after two years as its graphic designer, founded the ISTT Photographic Society, and mentored a team at FarhanasBrainstation on an education initiative. These are the lessons that stuck.

Photo: Group students table studying. View, CC0, via rawpixel.

1. Start with why the work matters

Volunteers don’t stay for tasks; they stay for purpose. At NUSDF, our team of four produced the forum’s brand communication and the visuals for five national skill development summits that reached more than 5,000 National University students across three divisions. When the team understood that a clear poster meant more students showed up to a session that might change their career, the late nights felt worth it.

Whenever I take on a new team, the first conversation is not about deadlines. It’s about who we’re doing this for and what changes if we do it well.

2. Make the work visible

In volunteer teams, effort easily goes unseen. Someone spends a weekend on a set of social posts and nobody mentions it. That’s how people quietly drift away.

I make a habit of:

  • crediting the designer by name when work goes out
  • sharing results (“this post reached X students”, “the hall was full”) with the whole team
  • showing early drafts in group chats so progress feels collective

Recognition costs nothing and is the main currency a volunteer leader has.

3. Design systems are leadership tools

One of the most effective things I did as a creative lead wasn’t a design at all. It was building templates and simple brand rules so that anyone on the team could produce on-brand work quickly.

When a summit needs speaker cards, schedules, countdown posts, certificates and banners, all in a week, you can’t design each one from scratch. With templates, a new volunteer can produce a speaker card in twenty minutes that looks like it came from the same team as everything else. That’s not just efficiency. It lets new people contribute confidently on their first day.

I wrote about the thinking behind this in Brand Identity Is More Than a Logo and Building a Personal Design System from One Colour.

4. Give clear briefs, then trust people

The fastest way to frustrate a creative volunteer is a vague request followed by endless revisions. The fastest way to frustrate a leader is to receive work that misses the point.

A good brief solves both. Mine usually fit in a few lines:

  • What: “Speaker announcement post, square, for Facebook and Instagram.”
  • Why: “To get students to register for the Chattogram session.”
  • Must include: name, title, photo, session time, registration link.
  • Deadline: with a clear first-draft date before the final one.

Then I step back. People do their best work when they own it, not when someone is looking over their shoulder in Illustrator.

5. Feedback that improves work without crushing people

Volunteers are often students still learning. Feedback has to make the work better and make the person want to come back.

What works for me:

  • Start with the goal, not taste. “The date is hard to find at a glance” is useful. “I don’t like it” is not.
  • Be specific. Point to the exact element and suggest a direction.
  • Limit the rounds. Two rounds of feedback, then decide. Endless iteration kills morale.
  • Explain the principle. If I explain why proximity or hierarchy matters, the next design is better without my help.

6. Plan backwards from the event

Events have a deadline that doesn’t move. When I coordinate event design, I plan backwards from the day:

  • Event day: banners, stage backdrop, live social posts.
  • One week before: schedule, speaker cards, reminder posts.
  • Two to three weeks before: announcement campaign and registration push.
  • Four weeks before: concept, key visual and templates locked.

The key visual and templates come first because everything else depends on them. Teams that design the backdrop the night before the event are teams that skipped this step.

7. Protect people from burnout

Volunteer teams burn out in predictable ways: the same two reliable people get every urgent task, and eventually they stop answering messages.

I try to spread work deliberately, pair experienced members with newer ones, and say no to requests that arrive too late to do well. A leader who says yes to everything is quietly volunteering their team’s weekends.

8. Build the next leaders

The best measure of a volunteer leader is what happens after they leave. Student organisations turn over every year. If all the knowledge lives in one person’s head, the team starts from zero every time.

So I document: how we brief, where templates live, which printers are reliable, what went wrong last time. And I give newer members real responsibility early, so that when it’s their turn to lead, they’ve already done it once with support.

What carries over to paid work

These lessons turned out to be just as useful outside student organisations. In my work at Channel i, clear written procedures and calm handovers matter as much as they did at any summit; I wrote about that in Inside a Master Control Room. When I run training sessions, such as an MS Office 365 and Google Workspace session for a leadership fellowship cohort, the same principles apply: start with why, keep it practical, and give people something they can use the next day.

Leadership in volunteer teams strips away formal authority. What’s left is clarity, recognition and trust. In my experience, those are what make any team work.

Summary

  • Start with why the work matters.
  • Make work visible on one shared board.
  • Use a design system as a leadership tool.
  • Give clear briefs, then trust people.
  • Plan backwards from the event, prevent burnout and build the next leaders.
